title: Reflection: shiny and dull surfaces, and seeing round corners with mirrors

summary.text: A white wall and a mirror both bounce back the light that lands on them, yet you see your face in only one of them. Breathe on a steel tumbler and your face vanishes at once, then returns as the fog clears. A polished plate can flash a spot of sunlight across a bay, while a dull pot cannot. In this unit your child maps where light goes after it hits a mirror, foil, paper and cloth. They find out how to turn a dull surface into a shiny one, and why a reflective strip on a school bag glows back at a torch. They build a periscope that sees over a wall, and learn that a wall and a mirror obey exactly the same rule.
summary.art: A child breathing on a steel tumbler where half the face has gone foggy, a white wall beside it, and a milk-carton periscope peeping over a garden wall.

intro.hook: Hold up a steel tumbler and look at your face in the shiny side. Breathe on it. Your face vanishes into fog. Wait a few seconds. Your face comes back. The steel did not change. What did the fog do to the light?
intro.text: Every surface sends back some of the light that lands on it. What is different is how tidily it does it. A mirror sends light back in neat order, so you see a picture. A wall sends it back in every direction, so you see the wall itself, from anywhere in the room. In this unit you find out why, and how polish, water and tape turn a dull surface into a shiny one. You also learn how two mirrors can send light round two corners, which is how a periscope lets you see over a wall.
intro.art: A steel tumbler with a clear reflection on one side and a foggy patch where the reflection has gone, and a ray of light drawn bouncing neatly off one side and scattering off the other.

outcomes: I can explain that every surface reflects some light, and that a smooth surface sends it back in order while a rough surface scatters it in every direction.
I can map where light goes after it hits a mirror, foil, paper and cloth, and say which surfaces I could see the lit spot on from many places.
I can explain that a rough surface still obeys the rule of reflection at each of its tiny bumps.
I can turn a dull surface into a shiny one, and explain how polish, wax, water and tape smooth the bumps.
I can explain why every surface turns mirror-like when I look at it from a very low angle, and why wet roads glare at night.
I can build a periscope with two mirrors, and explain why it shows the picture upright and not turned round.
I can explain why two or three mirrors at right angles send light straight back, as in a cat's eye on a road.
I can say how a curved mirror gathers or spreads light, and where people use them.

terms.meaning: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. Every surface reflects some of the light that lands on it.
terms.example: You see a book because light reflects off the book into your eyes.
terms.art: A ray of light hitting a book and bouncing toward an eye.

terms.meaning: Mirror-like reflection is when a very smooth surface sends light back in neat order, all the rays going the same way together. It makes a clear image.
terms.example: A bathroom mirror and still water in a bowl give mirror-like reflection.
terms.art: Three parallel rays hitting a mirror and leaving together in a neat bundle.

terms.meaning: Scattered reflection is when a rough surface sends light back in every direction. It makes no clear image, but lets you see the surface from anywhere.
terms.example: A white wall scatters light, so you can see the wall from any corner of the room.
terms.art: Three parallel rays hitting a bumpy surface and leaving in many different directions.

terms.meaning: An image is a picture that light makes of something, such as your face in a mirror. In a mirror, the image seems to be behind the glass.
terms.example: Your face in a mirror is an image made by light that bounced off you and then off the mirror.
terms.art: A child in front of a mirror, with a dotted copy of the child behind the glass.

terms.meaning: A ray is a thin line that shows the path of light. Light travels in straight lines until it hits something.
terms.example: A ray of sunlight through a gap in a curtain looks like a straight bright line in dusty air.
terms.art: A straight bright line of sunlight coming through a curtain gap, with dust in the beam.

terms.meaning: A surface is the outside of a thing, where it meets the air or another thing. Reflection happens at the surface.
terms.example: The surface of a steel tumbler is smooth. The surface of a coconut shell is rough.
terms.art: A smooth steel tumbler beside a rough coconut shell.

terms.meaning: A matt surface looks dull and does not show a clear picture of anything. Its tiny bumps scatter the light.
terms.example: Chalk, plain cloth and unpolished wood are matt.
terms.art: A piece of chalk and a plain cotton cloth, both looking dull.

terms.meaning: A glossy surface is shiny. It sends back part of the light in an orderly way, so you can see bright reflections in it.
terms.example: A glossy magazine page shows a bright reflection of a lamp.
terms.art: A glossy magazine page with a bright white patch where a lamp is reflected.

terms.meaning: To polish a surface is to rub it until the tiny bumps are smoothed down. A polished surface reflects more neatly and looks shinier.
terms.example: Polishing a brass lamp makes it shine.
terms.art: A hand with a cloth rubbing a brass lamp, with one half shiny and one half dull.

terms.meaning: Glare is a very bright reflection that is hard to look at. It happens when light bounces off a smooth surface straight into your eyes.
terms.example: The Sun's glare off a wet road or a lake makes you squint.
terms.art: A wet road at sunset with a blinding streak of reflected light running toward the viewer.

terms.meaning: A periscope is a tube with two mirrors that lets you see round a corner or over something. Light bounces off the top mirror, then off the lower mirror, into your eye.
terms.example: A submarine has a periscope to look above the water while the submarine stays below.
terms.art: A tall periscope tube with a mirror at each end, with a ray of light zigzagging down the tube.

terms.meaning: A retroreflector is a set of mirror surfaces at right angles that sends light straight back to where it came from.
terms.example: A bicycle reflector is a retroreflector. It glows back when car headlights hit it.
terms.art: A bicycle reflector at night, with a beam from a car headlight returning along the same path.

terms.meaning: A concave mirror curves inward, like the inside of a spoon. It gathers light to a small bright spot.
terms.example: A solar cooker dish is a concave mirror that gathers sunlight onto a pot.
terms.art: A curved dish mirror with parallel rays coming in and meeting at one bright point.

terms.meaning: A convex mirror curves outward, like the back of a spoon. It spreads light out and shows a wide view, in a smaller size.
terms.example: A shop's corner mirror is convex, so the shopkeeper can see the whole shop.
terms.art: A round mirror bulging outward in the corner of a shop, showing the whole aisle.

terms.meaning: The focus of a mirror is the spot where it gathers rays together. A focus is very bright because the light is packed into a small space.
terms.example: A curved steel katori held in a torch beam gathers light into a bright spot on a card.
terms.art: A katori bowl with a torch beam and a bright small spot on a card in front of it.

terms.meaning: An optical fibre is a thin strand of glass that carries light along inside it, even round bends. The light bounces along the inside walls.
terms.example: Internet messages travel as flashes of light along optical fibres under the sea.
terms.art: A thin glass strand curving through a ring, with a ray bouncing along the inside.

terms.meaning: A reflecting telescope uses a big curved mirror, instead of a big glass lens, to gather the light from faraway things.
terms.example: Isaac Newton built a small reflecting telescope in 1668.
terms.art: A telescope tube with a big curved mirror at the bottom and a small eyepiece on the side.

terms.meaning: A beam is a narrow stream of light going in one direction. A torch with a slit, or a laser, makes a beam.
terms.example: A torch through a card with a thin slit makes a narrow beam you can follow across a table.
terms.art: A torch shining through a slit in a card, making a thin line of light across a sheet of paper.

terms.meaning: Albedo is the share of the light that lands on a surface that the surface sends back. A mirror has a high albedo, and black cloth has a low one.
terms.example: Fresh snow has a high albedo. Dark tar has a low one.
terms.art: A bright snowfield beside a patch of dark tar, with arrows showing more light returning from the snow.

terms.meaning: A solar cooker uses mirrors to gather sunlight onto a pot, to heat food without fuel.
terms.example: A box cooker with a shiny lid can bake rice on a sunny day in Bengaluru.
terms.art: A box solar cooker with a shiny lid propped open and a black pot inside.

explanations.definition: When light lands on any surface, some of it bounces off. The bounced light is what lets you see the surface.
explanations.description: A mirror is not special because it reflects. Everything reflects. A wall, a banana, a school bag and your own hand all send some of the light that lands on them into the room. That is the only reason you can see them. They make no light of their own. A thing that reflected nothing at all would be invisible, and you would see only what is behind it. So the real question about a surface is not whether it reflects, but how it does it. Some surfaces send the light back in neat order. Others scatter it in every direction.
examples: A dark cloth still reflects a little light, which is why you can see its folds.
The Moon makes no light. It shines because it reflects sunlight.
You see a friend across the room because light reflected off your friend reaches your eyes.
explanations.art: A room with a lamp and rays going to a wall, a book and a banana, and from each of them to a child's eyes.

explanations.definition: A very smooth surface sends light back in neat order and makes an image. A rough surface scatters light in all directions and makes no image, but can be seen from anywhere.
explanations.description: Picture a bundle of parallel rays landing on a mirror. They all meet a flat surface, so they all bounce off together, in the same new direction. Your eye, in the right place, collects the whole bundle and sees a picture. Now picture the same rays landing on white paper. Under a microscope, paper is a tangle of tiny fibres, with bumps and slopes facing every way. Each ray meets a differently tilted bump, so each bounces off in a different direction. The light is scattered. No picture forms, but light leaves the paper in every direction, so you can see the paper from any side of the room.
examples: A bathroom mirror and still water give a clear image of your face.
A white wall scatters light, and looks the same from every corner of a room.
A glossy magazine page does a bit of both: you can see a bright patch of lamp in it, and you can also read the page from any angle.
explanations.art: Two side-by-side drawings: parallel rays leaving a smooth mirror together, and the same rays leaving a bumpy surface in many different directions.

explanations.concept: The same rule works on every tiny bump
explanations.definition: Light leaves a flat surface at the same angle that it arrives. A rough surface is made of tiny flat patches tilted every way, and each patch follows the rule.
explanations.description: In Class 3, you learned that a ray leaves a flat mirror at the same angle that it arrives. This is the rule of reflection. A rough surface does not break the rule. Look at one tiny patch of a rough surface, so small that it is flat. On that patch, the ray leaves at the same angle it arrived, measured against that patch. But the next patch is tilted differently, so its ray goes off somewhere else. A wall is a huge number of tiny mirrors tilted every which way. A mirror is a huge number of tiny patches all lying flat together. The rule is the same. The only difference is how well the patches line up.
examples: Crumpled foil sparkles in every direction, because each little flat fold sends light its own way.
A sheet of paper looks the same brightness from every side, because its bumps face every way.
A smooth steel tumbler shows a clear face, because its surface is a long, even curve.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in drawing of a bumpy wall surface with each tiny patch shown as a short flat line and a ray bouncing off it at the same angle.

explanations.concept: How big a bump can be before it spoils the mirror
explanations.definition: A surface acts like a mirror when its bumps are much smaller than the wavelength of light, about half a thousandth of a millimetre.
explanations.description: Light is a wave. A wave cannot 'feel' a bump that is far smaller than the length of the wave itself. Visible light has a wavelength of about 0.0005 millimetres. If a surface's bumps are much smaller than that, the light sees the surface as flat, and the surface works like a mirror. If the bumps are bigger, light sees every bump and scatters. So the same material can be a mirror or a wall, depending on how finely it is polished. A mirror-makers' polish is smooth to a tiny fraction of a wavelength. Ordinary paper has bumps many times bigger than that, so it scatters.
examples: Rubbing a dull metal tray with fine polish makes it shine, because it wears down the bumps.
The same sheet of glass can be clear and shiny, or frosted and dull if its surface is roughened.
A very fine mirror for a telescope is polished so smooth that its bumps are tiny compared with a wavelength of light.
explanations.art: A magnified drawing of a bumpy surface next to a smooth one, with a wavy line of light about the size of the bumps on the left and much bigger than the bumps on the right.

explanations.concept: How polish, wax, water and tape make a surface shine
explanations.definition: Polish, wax, water and clear tape all fill or flatten the tiny bumps on a surface, so the surface reflects in order and looks shinier.
explanations.description: Shoe polish and car wax fill the tiny dips in a surface with a smooth layer, and rubbing flattens the top. A thin film of water or oil does a similar thing, by filling the dips with a layer that is smooth on top. Clear tape lays a very flat skin over everything. In every case, the bumps are hidden under a smooth top, so the light meets a flat surface. This is why a wet pebble looks brighter and deeper in colour than a dry one, why a shoeshine man's work makes leather shine, and why fog on a mirror spoils it. Fog is thousands of tiny drops, each one a bump that scatters the light.
examples: A shoeshine man's polish makes a dull black shoe gleam.
A wet stone looks shinier than a dry stone, because the water smooths the surface.
Fog on a bathroom mirror hides your face, because the droplets scatter the light.
explanations.art: A dull shoe on one side and a polished shoe on the other, with a zoomed-in circle on each showing bumps and a smooth layer.

explanations.concept: Every surface turns into a mirror at a low enough angle
explanations.definition: At a very low, glancing angle, even a dull surface reflects most of the light in an orderly way and shows a mirror-like image.
explanations.description: Try this with a plain page. Hold it level, with a lamp on the far side of the room. Look straight down, and the page looks matt. Now lower your head until your eye is almost level with the page and look across it. The page now shows a blurry bright image of the lamp. At a very shallow angle, the light skims across the tiny bumps instead of hitting them, so they behave like a smooth surface. This is why wet roads glare at night. Water on the road smooths it, and the street lights and the car headlights hit it at a glancing angle. A calm lake looks like a mirror at sunset for the same reason. Polarising sunglasses cut down this glare.
examples: A wet road at night shows long streaks of street lights.
A calm lake at sunrise shows the sky almost perfectly, though it is a poor mirror at noon.
A tiled floor shows the ceiling light when you look across it from low down.
explanations.art: An eye near the table surface looking across a plain white page, with a lamp's bright reflection on the far part of the page.

explanations.concept: How much light a surface sends back
explanations.definition: Every surface sends back only a share of the light that lands on it. The share is called its albedo. The rest is absorbed and turned into heat, or goes through.
explanations.description: A good mirror sends back about nine tenths of the light. Fresh white paper sends back most of it, about four fifths. Black cloth sends back only a small share, which is why it looks black and gets warm. The Moon is a good example. Its rock and dust are dark grey, and it sends back only about one eighth of the sunlight that lands on it. Yet that is enough to light up a whole night, because the Moon is huge and the light is scattered all round. Fresh snow has a high albedo, and so cools the ground below it. Dark forests and roads have a low albedo. The shares are rough numbers, because they change with the colour and the angle.
examples: White paper reflects most of the light and looks bright.
Black cloth reflects very little, looks dark and gets warm in the sun.
The Moon sends back only about one eighth of the sunlight that lands on it.
explanations.art: A row of four squares, a mirror, white paper, black cloth and the Moon, each with a number of arrows leaving to show how much light is sent back.

explanations.definition: A periscope uses two mirrors, each tilted at 45 degrees, to send light round two right-angle turns, so you can see over or round something.
explanations.description: A mirror tilted at 45 degrees turns a ray through a right angle. In a periscope, light from a scene goes into the top window, hits the top mirror and turns down the tube. At the bottom, it hits the second mirror and turns again, out through the viewing window to your eye. You see the scene as if you were looking from the top of the tube. Two mirrors turn the picture twice. The first turn flips the picture, and the second flips it back. So the picture is upright and the right way round. Submarines used periscopes to look above the waves while the boat stayed hidden. Soldiers in trenches used them to look over the top without raising their heads.
examples: A submarine periscope lets the crew see ships on the surface.
A child with a cardboard periscope can see over a garden wall.
A periscope in a long hall lets a person see round a pillar.
explanations.art: A tall periscope beside a wall, with a ray from a boat on the far side going into the top window, bouncing twice and reaching an eye at the bottom.

explanations.concept: Corner mirrors that send light straight back
explanations.definition: Two mirrors set at a right angle, or three mirrors set like the corner of a box, send light back parallel to the way it came in. Such a device is called a retroreflector.
explanations.description: A single mirror sends a beam off at an angle. Two mirrors at a right angle make the beam bounce twice, and it comes out parallel to its path in, going back toward the torch. Three mirrors at right angles, like the inside corner of a cardboard box, do this for a beam from any direction. That is why a bicycle reflector, a cat's eye on a road and the reflective strip on a school bag glow when a headlight shines on them, as seen from near the headlight. Left on the Moon by astronauts in 1969, a set of corner reflectors still sends laser flashes back to Earth. India's Chandrayaan-3 lander, in 2023, carried one made by NASA.
examples: A cat's eye in the middle of a highway glows back at the driver.
A reflective strip on a school bag glows brightly in a torch beam, and can look dark in daylight.
Astronauts left corner reflectors on the Moon, and scientists still bounce lasers off them to measure the distance to the Moon.
explanations.art: Three mirrors forming the corner of a box with a beam of light going in and coming straight back along the same direction.

explanations.concept: Curved mirrors gather or spread light
explanations.definition: A concave mirror, curved inward, gathers parallel rays to a bright spot. A convex mirror, curved outward, spreads them and shows a wide view.
explanations.description: Every tiny patch of a curved mirror follows the rule of reflection, but the patches are tilted differently. On a concave mirror, the patches tilt so that the reflected rays cross at one spot, the focus. The light there is packed tight and bright. Solar cookers, torch reflectors and telescope mirrors use this. On a convex mirror, the patches tilt away from each other, so the rays spread out. You see a wide view, but small. Shop corner mirrors and the side mirrors of cars are convex. Never use a curved mirror to focus sunlight at your hand, a person or a pet. The bright spot can burn skin and start fires.
examples: The inside of a steel katori gathers a torch beam to a small spot, and the back spreads it out.
Car headlights have a curved mirror behind the bulb, so most of the light goes forward in a beam.
A convex shop mirror shows the whole aisle at once.
explanations.art: A concave mirror with rays meeting at one point and a convex mirror with the same rays spreading out.

explanations.concept: Light trapped inside glass: optical fibres
explanations.definition: Light travelling along inside a thin glass strand bounces off the inside walls and stays in, even round bends. This is how an optical fibre carries a message.
explanations.description: When light inside glass hits the wall at a shallow angle, it is all reflected back in, and none escapes. This is called total internal reflection. Inside a thin strand of glass, the light keeps hitting the wall at shallow angles, so it zigzags along the whole length, bends and all. Narinder Singh Kapany, a physicist born in Punjab, did early work in the 1950s that helped to show that light could be carried this way, and he is remembered for naming the field fibre optics. Today, internet messages travel as flashes of light along fibres on the sea floor. Doctors use bundles of fibres to look inside the body.
examples: Internet cables under the sea are optical fibres, carrying flashes of light.
Doctors can look inside the stomach with a thin tube of optical fibres.
A light-up toy with glowing threads at the ends is made of optical fibres.
explanations.art: A thin glass strand bent into a curve, with a ray of light bouncing along the inside walls from one end to the other.

explanations.definition: Many living beings have mirrors in their bodies, to see, to hide or to shine.
explanations.description: A scallop has dozens of tiny eyes along the edge of their shell. In 1965, Michael Land, a British scientist, showed that each eye has a curved mirror at the back that gathers light to form an image. Many silvery fish, such as sardines, have tiny crystals in their scales that act as mirrors. In open water, these scales reflect the light around the fish, which makes the fish hard for hunters to see. Cats have a mirror layer behind the retina, which sends light back through the eye for a second chance to be caught. That is why a cat's eyes shine in a torch beam. Some beetles and butterflies have shining wings that are not coloured by paint. Their surface structure reflects only certain colours.
examples: A scallop's eyes use a curved mirror to make an image.
A sardine's silver sides reflect the water around them.
A cat's eyes glow green or yellow in a torch beam at night.
explanations.art: A scallop with a row of small blue eyes along the edge of the shell, and a cutaway of one eye showing a curved mirror at the back.

explanations.concept: Should we reflect sunlight away to cool the Earth?
explanations.description: The Earth is warming because we are adding gases such as carbon dioxide that hold in heat. Some scientists have asked a bold question: could we send some sunlight back into space before it warms us? Ideas include painting roofs white, putting tiny shiny particles in the high air, and even huge mirrors in space. Each idea reflects some sunlight, so each would cool the Earth a little. But no one has tested the big ideas, and they carry risks nobody fully understands. People disagree about whether to even try them. Painting roofs and pavements white and light is the least risky, and it is already being done in some hot cities.
examples: Painting roofs white in a hot city can lower the temperature inside buildings.
A volcano that throws dust high into the air can cool the Earth for a year or two, because the dust reflects sunlight.
Fresh snow reflects most sunlight, so melting snow makes the Earth absorb more.
explanations.art: The Earth with a thin shiny haze around it, and arrows of sunlight bouncing off the haze back into space.

perspectives.explanation: The warming is serious and the cuts to carbon dioxide are slow. We should study reflecting some sunlight carefully, so that people have the facts if they ever need them.
Reflecting sunlight would not remove the carbon dioxide. It might change rainfall, including the monsoon, in ways we cannot predict. And if it stopped suddenly, the Earth could warm quickly.
The first job is to cut the gases that cause the warming. Reflecting sunlight, at the most, should come after that and be done only with every country having a say.

agreed.text: Every surface reflects some of the light that lands on it, and that reflected light is what lets us see things that make no light of their own.
agreed.evidence: You can see unlit objects in a room with a lamp, and cameras record them. In a room with no light at all, nothing is seen.

agreed.text: A smooth surface sends light back in order and makes an image. A rough surface scatters light in all directions.
agreed.evidence: A mirror shows a clear image of a torch only from one place. White paper, lit by the same torch, can be seen from any place around it.

agreed.text: Light follows the same rule of reflection on every flat patch of a surface, rough or smooth.
agreed.evidence: Looking at a surface under a microscope, each tiny patch bounces a thin beam at the matching angle. Laser tests on rough and smooth surfaces agree with this.

agreed.text: Polishing, waxing or wetting a surface can make it shinier, because it smooths the bumps.
agreed.evidence: Measurements of surfaces before and after polishing show smoother surfaces, and the reflected light becomes more orderly.

agreed.text: At a very low angle, even rough surfaces reflect most of the light in an orderly way.
agreed.evidence: Wet roads, lakes and glossy paper all show mirror-like reflections when seen at a shallow angle, and the effect is measured in labs.

agreed.text: Two mirrors at 45 degrees make a periscope that shows an upright picture, and corner mirrors at right angles send light straight back.
agreed.evidence: Submarines, bicycle reflectors, cat's eyes and the reflectors left on the Moon all work this way, and anyone can test them with a torch.

agreed.text: A concave mirror gathers light to a focus, and a convex mirror spreads it out.
agreed.evidence: Telescopes with curved mirrors, solar cookers, car headlights and shop mirrors all work, and a katori and a torch show it at home.

challenging.claim: Mirrors reflect light, but walls and paper do not.
challenging.who: Many people, because mirrors show pictures and walls do not.
challenging.for: You see your face in a mirror but not in a white wall, so it feels as if only the mirror bounces light.
challenging.against: You can see a white wall only because it reflects light into your eyes. A wall scatters the light in every direction instead of in one tidy direction. It reflects, but it does not make an image.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that only mirrors reflect light, and why a wall reflects too.

challenging.claim: A rough surface breaks the rule that light bounces off at the same angle it arrives.
challenging.who: Many students, who see light scatter off paper and think the rule has failed.
challenging.for: On a rough surface the rays go off in all directions, not just one.
challenging.against: The rule holds on every tiny flat patch. The patches face different ways, so the rays go in different directions. Nothing is broken. The surface is simply a huge number of tiny mirrors tilted every way.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the rule of reflection stops working on rough surfaces.

challenging.claim: A black thing reflects no light at all.
challenging.who: Many people, because black things look so dark.
challenging.for: A black cloth or black paint looks dark, so it seems to send nothing back.
challenging.against: Black cloth still sends back a small share, which is why you can see its folds. Some modern black materials take in more than 99.9 parts in 100 of the light, but nothing takes in absolutely all of it.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a black thing reflects any light at all.

challenging.claim: A periscope turns the picture upside down or back to front.
challenging.who: Some people, because they have seen pictures turned round in a spoon or a single mirror.
challenging.for: A single mirror turns a picture back to front, and a lens can turn it upside down.
challenging.against: A periscope uses two mirrors. The first mirror flips the picture and the second flips it back. The two flips cancel, so the picture comes out upright and the right way round.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a periscope shows things upside down or reversed.

challenging.claim: Archimedes burned the Roman fleet at Syracuse using a ring of mirrors or shiny shields.
challenging.who: Writers who lived hundreds of years after Archimedes, such as Lucian, wrote about it, and many people since have repeated it.
challenging.for: A big curved mirror can focus sunlight to a hot spot. Some modern tests have lit wood at short range after several minutes.
challenging.against: The earliest writers who describe the siege do not mention it. Ships move, the Sun is not a point and the spot is hard to hold in place. Most historians doubt the story, though it remains a famous idea.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous old story, that Archimedes used mirrors as a weapon, and whether it could be true.

challenging.claim: Telescopes with a big glass lens are the best way to see faint stars.
challenging.who: Most astronomers before 1668, and many popular books since.
challenging.for: The first telescopes used lenses, and lenses are easy to understand.
challenging.against: A big lens bends different colours by different amounts, so images get coloured fringes. A mirror bounces all colours the same way. Almost every big telescope today is a reflecting telescope with a huge curved mirror.
challenging.context: This card is about telescopes, and why mirrors beat lenses for the biggest ones.

big_questions.q: A white wall reflects the light of a lamp, but it does not show your face. Where did the picture of your face go?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens to a bundle of rays that lands on a bumpy surface. Does it stay in order?

big_questions.q: The Moon reflects only about one eighth of the sunlight that lands on it, yet it lights up the night. If the Moon were a perfect mirror ball, would the night be brighter or darker?
big_questions.hint: A mirror ball sends each ray in one direction. Imagine standing on the Earth and looking for the bright spot.

big_questions.q: You see your friends only by the light that scatters off them, and you see yourself in a mirror by tidy light. Is the face you see in a mirror the same face your friends see?
big_questions.hint: A mirror turns front to back. Think about the photographs you have seen of yourself, and which feels more like you.

big_questions.q: If you could make a surface perfectly smooth, down to single atoms, would it look like anything at all?
big_questions.hint: A perfect mirror shows only the things in front of it. Can you see the mirror itself?

big_questions.q: Light carries a little news from every surface it bounces off. Is the light in a room a kind of record of everything it has touched?
big_questions.hint: The colour of a red apple is in the light that reaches your eye. What else is in it?

big_questions.q: James Gregory designed a reflecting telescope in 1663, but could not make it work. Isaac Newton built one in 1668. Who invented the reflecting telescope?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between an idea, a design and a working machine. Who should get the credit for each?

big_questions.q: Reflectors left on the Moon in 1969 still send laser flashes back to us. Which of the things people make today might still be working in a thousand years?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the reflectors have in common. They have no batteries, no moving parts and nothing to wear out.

big_questions.q: Should the world try to cool the Earth by reflecting sunlight away, or only by cutting the gases that warm it?

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1660s, telescopes used glass lenses. They had a problem. Stars and planets looked blurry, with coloured fringes. Many thinkers, including Descartes, believed this came from lenses not being ground to quite the right shape, and that better grinding would cure it. In 1666, Isaac Newton let a thin beam of sunlight through a glass prism. He found that white light is a mixture of colours, and that glass bends each colour by a different amount. So no lens shape could bring all the colours to one point. But a mirror bounces every colour at the same angle. In 1668 Newton built a small telescope with a curved metal mirror in place of the big lens. It showed no coloured fringes. He showed it to the Royal Society in London in 1671. Almost all the largest telescopes built since then use mirrors.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many thinkers believed that the coloured blur in telescopes came from badly shaped lenses, and that perfect grinding would cure it. Newton showed that glass bends colours by different amounts, so no shape can fix it, but a mirror treats all colours alike.

story.title: The Plate That Called the Shore
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. A smooth, polished surface sends a flash of sunlight in one direction, and a dull, scratched one scatters it. People at sea have long used mirrors to flash sunlight as a signal, and three short flashes, three long and three short is the well-known call for help. The Gulf of Mannar and Rameswaram are real places. Selvi, her family and everything they say and do are made up.
text: Kalaivani Amma was one of the few women in Rameswaram who took her own boat out to sea. In the school holidays, she took her daughter Selvi, who was ten, and her son Murugan, who was six.

One afternoon in the Gulf of Mannar, the engine coughed twice and died. Kalaivani Amma pulled the starter cord until her arm ached. It would not start again. The sea was calm, but a slow current was pushing the boat away from the land.

Her phone was dead. She had forgotten to charge it. Selvi's torch was at home in her school bag. The shore was a thin brown line. The lighthouse was a pale pencil mark. The Sun was low and off to one side, turning the water orange.
'The shore is much too far,' said his mother. 'Nobody would hear us.'

Selvi looked at what they had. There was a coil of rope. There was a fish basket. There was an aluminium pot for making tea. There was a steel plate from lunch. She thought of her teacher, Miss Fernandez, who had once shown the class how a small mirror could throw a bright spot of sunlight across the playground. 'Light bounces off a smooth surface like a ball off a wall,' Miss Fernandez had said. 'It leaves at the same angle it arrives. So you can aim it.'

Selvi picked up the aluminium pot first. It was big, and she thought it would catch more sun. She turned it toward the Sun. The pot glowed a soft orange all over. She tilted it this way and that. The glow stayed soft and spread out. It lit up her own face, and the side of the boat. That was all.
'It shines nicely,' said her mother. 'But nobody on shore would notice it.'

Selvi turned the pot over and looked at the outside. It was scratched all over by years of use. There were hundreds of tiny dents and lines. 'Every dent bounces the light somewhere different,' she said slowly. 'So it sends light everywhere. And that means it sends it nowhere in particular.'

She put down the pot and picked up the steel plate. Kalaivani Amma scrubbed it every day with ash and a bit of tamarind, until it was smooth and bright. Selvi held it out toward the Sun. A round coin of dazzling white light leapt onto the wooden side of the boat. She tipped the plate a tiny bit. The spot of light jumped all the way across the boat and onto the water.
'It moves a lot when I move the plate a little,' she said. 'That is how a ball bounces. A tiny turn makes a big change.'

Now she had to aim. She remembered the trick Miss Fernandez had taught them. She held out her other hand with two fingers in a V, in front of her. She tilted the plate until the bright spot sat on the tip of one finger. Then she moved her whole hand until the V pointed straight at the white lighthouse on the shore. She slid the spot of light along her fingers, and then off the tip, and out along the line toward the land.

She could not see where the spot landed, a long way off. She only knew that it was going in the right direction. Murugan stood beside her and counted. She covered the plate with her palm and uncovered it, to make short flashes and long flashes. She made three short, then three long, then three short. It was the old call for help that Miss Fernandez had told them sailors used.

The Sun slid lower. Her arm ached. The flashes got fainter, because the Sun was low and the light that fell on the plate was thinner. Her mother took the plate and held it while Selvi rested her arm, and then Selvi took it back. They kept it going, three short, three long, three short.

Far to the north, a bigger fishing boat was heading home. At the front stood Mary Akka, a friend of Kalaivani Amma, in a red scarf. She saw something strange. It was a small white star, blinking low over the sea, at a time of day when no stars were out. Three short blinks, three long blinks, three short blinks. She stared at it for a moment. Then she shouted to her crew, and the big boat turned.
That evening, Kalaivani Amma and the children were towed back into Rameswaram harbour with the lamps coming on all along the shore.

The next day Miss Fernandez asked Selvi what she had done. 'I used the plate,' said Selvi. 'The plate is smooth. The pot is covered in tiny dents. A smooth surface bounces all the light the same way, so it can be aimed in one beam. A rough surface bounces it every which way, so it just glows.'
'And why does the same rule work on both?' asked Miss Fernandez.
Selvi thought about it. 'Because each dent is a tiny mirror too,' she said. 'It just faces the wrong way.'
story.epiphany: A smooth plate sends sunlight off in one direction, so it can be aimed far away. A scratched pot scatters the same sunlight everywhere, so it only glows.

roots.context: We found out that every surface reflects, and that the only difference is how tidily it does it. Now we ask what that tells us about seeing the world and ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: A white wall and a mirror both bounce light off at the same angle. The wall is made of tiny bumps facing every way. So it sends light everywhere, and you see the wall itself.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'mirrors reflect' as if walls, paper and people did not. We only notice reflection when it makes a picture.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Where Does the Bounce Go test, the mirror showed its lit spot from one place only, and the white paper showed its spot from every place. Both followed the rule. If your results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: You see your friends only because light scatters off them into your eyes. A mirror is the only time you see your own face with tidy light.
three.what_is_life: A scallop sees with tiny curved mirrors at the back of their eyes. A sardine hides by reflecting the water around her. Many living beings use reflection to see or to hide.
three.what_is_this_world: Almost everything you have ever seen was scattered light. The Moon, the page of a book and a friend's face are all lit by light that bounced off them.

roots.thread: A mirror and a wall do the same thing. Each tiny patch of a surface bounces light by the same rule. The patches of a mirror line up. The patches of a wall face every way. So a mirror shows one picture, and a wall shows itself to the whole room. Almost all that we see of the world is light scattered by rough surfaces. The tidy picture in a mirror is the rare case.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the net of Indra
teachings.teaching: This Buddhist teaching describes a net hung over the world, with a bright jewel at each knot. Each jewel reflects every other jewel in the net, and each of those jewels reflects all the others again, without end.
teachings.link: Two mirrors facing each other make endless copies, and every bumpy patch of a wall bounces a little of the whole room. Each place holds a trace of all the others.

teachings.source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book 1 (the Greek and the Chinese painters)
teachings.teaching: In a story told by Rumi, a Persian poet, painters from Greece and from China each decorated one side of a room. The Chinese painters used many colours. The Greek painters only polished their wall until it shone like a mirror. When the curtain between them was drawn back, the polished wall showed the Chinese painting, even more beautiful than before.
teachings.link: The Greek painters did not paint anything. They polished the bumps away until the wall could show everything in front of it. Polishing turned a wall that only scattered light into a surface that could hold a clear picture.

science.text: Light follows the same rule of reflection at every tiny patch of every surface. Smooth surfaces send the light back in order, and rough surfaces scatter it.
A surface acts as a mirror when its bumps are much smaller than the wavelength of light, about half a thousandth of a millimetre.
Whether we should reflect sunlight away from the Earth to cool it is debated, and no one has tested the big ideas.

other_view.view: A mirror and a wall differ only in the size of their bumps. The tale of 'tidy light' and 'scattered light' is a way of talking about bump size. Nothing deeper about seeing or about oneself needs to be read into it. This is an honest view.

practice.title: Fog and clear
practice.say: Take a clean steel tumbler, or a small mirror. Look at your eyes in it. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out onto the steel, and watch your face vanish into fog. Breathe in slowly again. Wait, and watch the fog fade. Your face comes back. Breathe out and in a few more times. Think about how the light was always there. Only the bumps changed.
practice.kid: Look at your eyes in a steel tumbler. Breathe out onto it. Watch the fog. Wait and watch your face come back.

ask: A white wall reflects as much light as a mirror, yet it shows no picture. Is that because the wall is hiding something, or because it shows everything at once?
When you see your face in a mirror, who is looking at whom?
If everything we see is scattered light, do we ever see a thing as it is, or only what it does to light?

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a surface on the front, the answer and the reason on the back

items.f: A bathroom mirror with a clean glass front.
items.b: Clear image. The glass is polished so smooth that its bumps are far smaller than a wavelength of light. All the rays leave in order, so you see a sharp image.

items.f: Still water in a steel basin on a windless day.
items.b: Clear image. The top of still water is a flat, smooth sheet. It sends rays back in order, so it shows a clear image of the sky.

items.f: A polished steel thali that has just been scrubbed with ash.
items.b: Clear image. Scrubbing wears away the bumps. A smooth steel face reflects in order, so you can see your face in it.

items.f: The glass of a framed photograph hung on a wall.
items.b: Clear image. Glass is very smooth. It reflects some light in order, which is why you see the window in it as a glare.

items.f: A calm pond at sunrise.
items.b: Clear image. Calm water is smooth, and the Sun is low, which is a glancing angle. Both help to make a clear image of the trees.

items.f: The black screen of a switched-off phone.
items.b: Clear image. A smooth glass screen with nothing glowing behind it reflects like a mirror. You can see your face in it.

items.f: A shiny steel tumbler, seen from the front.
items.b: Clear image. Steel is smooth. The curve bends the image, so your face looks stretched, but the image is clear.

items.f: A polished marble floor in a temple.
items.b: Clear image. Polishing smooths the marble until the lamps above show in it as clear, bright shapes.

items.f: A glossy magazine page, held under a lamp.
items.b: Blurry or partial image. The page has a smooth coating, so it gives a bright patch of the lamp. But it is not smooth enough for a full image, so the patch is soft.

items.f: A polished wooden table with a coat of varnish.
items.b: Blurry or partial image. Varnish fills many bumps, so the table shows a soft image of the window. Some bumps remain, so the image is blurred.

items.f: A wet road at night, with the street lights shining on it.
items.b: Blurry or partial image. Water fills the bumps, and the lights hit it at a glancing angle. So you see long streaks of light, though not a sharp image.

items.f: A one-rupee coin that has been in many pockets.
items.b: Blurry or partial image. The coin is metal and fairly smooth, but it is scratched and worn. It shows a bright patch and a fuzzy image.

items.f: A brass lamp that has not been polished for a month.
items.b: Blurry or partial image. The brass is smooth underneath, but a dull layer covers it. You see a faint, smeared image.

items.f: A steel spoon with lots of fine scratches.
items.b: Blurry or partial image. The scratches scatter part of the light. The rest is still reflected in order, so the image is there but hazy.

items.f: A new bicycle frame painted with glossy paint.
items.b: Blurry or partial image. Gloss paint is smooth but not perfectly flat. It gives bright patches and soft images.

items.f: A steel tray, rubbed with fine sandpaper.
items.b: Blurry or partial image. Sandpaper adds fine scratches. The steel still reflects in order a little, but it is hazy.

items.f: A white wall.
items.b: No image. The wall is made of tiny bumps facing every way. Each bump bounces light somewhere different, so there is no image. But you can see the wall from anywhere.

items.f: A sheet of plain white paper.
items.b: No image. Paper is a tangle of tiny fibres. It scatters the light in every direction, so there is no image of anything.

items.f: A cotton shirt.
items.b: No image. Cloth is made of threads with gaps and fuzz. It scatters light every which way, so you cannot see yourself in it.

items.f: A clay matka for water.
items.b: No image. Baked clay has a rough surface that scatters light. It makes no image, but it is easy to see.

items.f: A rough brick wall.
items.b: No image. The brick is full of bumps and holes that scatter light in every direction. It shows no image.

items.f: The Moon in the night sky.
items.b: No image. The Moon's dust and rock scatter sunlight in every direction. That is why the whole Moon glows. A mirror Moon would show only a tiny bright dot.

items.f: A bathroom mirror covered in fog after a hot shower.
items.b: No image. The fog is thousands of tiny water drops that scatter the light. The smooth glass underneath can no longer make an image.

items.f: A chalkboard wiped with a dry cloth.
items.b: No image. Chalk dust is a rough powder, which scatters light. A dull board shows no image, which is good for reading what is written on it.

printables.title: Paper stars, buttons or coins for points (40 are enough)
items: Cut out 40 small paper stars, or use buttons or coins

rules: Lay the 3 signs in a row. Shuffle the 24 cards and make a face-down pile. Put the 40 stars in a heap in the middle.
On your turn, take the top card and read the front aloud. Do not read the back.
Choose a sign for the card and say why in one sentence. Use the words smooth, rough or bumps. Put the card under that sign.

Heat it in the Sun
Make it bigger
