If you have the exit right, take 2 stars. If you also have the number of turns right, take 1 more star.
Play all 12 cards, or as many as you like. The player with the most stars wins. If you tie, you share the win.
Playing alone: score 3 stars for each card you get fully right. Try for 30 or more.

flow.do: Cut out the cards, the key and the tokens. Draw the 5 by 5 grid. Read the key together.
flow.say: A mirror turns a beam through a right angle. A mirror that leans right sends a beam going right upward. Let's check the key on the board.
flow.kid: Draw the grid. Read the key for R and L.
flow.context: This is the first step of Mirror Maze. You draw the grid and learn the key.

ask.q: A beam going right meets a mirror leaning right. Which way does it go?

flow.parent: Draw a slash and a backslash on a bit of paper, and use a pencil as a beam. It is easier to see the turn with a real pencil. A real mirror leaning at 45 degrees turns a beam through a right angle.

flow.do: Try Maze 1 together. Copy it to the grid, trace the beam and check the back.
flow.say: Put your finger where the beam enters. Go straight until a mirror. Which way does it turn? Keep going until it leaves.
flow.kid: Trace the first maze with your finger. Where does the beam leave?
flow.context: In this step, you trace the first maze together and see how it works.

check.q: A beam travelling down meets a mirror leaning left, which is a backslash. Which way does it go?
options: Right
Left
Up
It carries on down
check.why: A beam going down and meeting a backslash turns to the right. Picture a ball rolling down onto a backslash. It is knocked off toward the right. If you picked 'left', you may have used the slash rule by mistake.

flow.do: Take turns with the cards. Each player copies the maze, traces the beam, says the exit and the turns, then reads the back.
flow.say: Copy the mirrors. Trace the beam. Tell us where it leaves and how many times it turned. Then check the back.
flow.kid: Take turns. Trace each maze. Say where the beam leaves.
flow.context: In this step, you play the main part of Mirror Maze.
flow.parent: If your child gets lost, trace with a pencil on the grid and mark each turn with a dot. Check the first turn together, then let them carry on.
flow.think: If you swapped every slash for a backslash in a maze, would the beam leave in the same place?

flow.do: Make your own maze. Put in six mirrors, choose where the beam enters and work out where it leaves. Swap with someone to check.
flow.say: Now you are the puzzle maker. Draw six mirrors, pick where the beam enters, and work out where it leaves. Then give it to someone else.
flow.kid: Make your own maze with six mirrors. Swap with someone.
flow.context: In this step, you make a maze of your own for someone else to solve.

check.q: In a maze, a beam enters at the left of row 2 and meets no mirrors at all. Where does it leave?
options: The right side of row 2
The top of column 5
The left side of row 5
It never leaves
check.why: With no mirrors, the beam goes straight on. It travels along row 2 and leaves at the right side of the same row. Light only changes direction when it meets something.

flow.do: Talk about where real mirrors turn beams, such as in a periscope.
flow.say: Which real thing is like these mazes? Where do mirrors turn a beam through right angles?
flow.kid: Where do real mirrors turn a beam through a right angle?
flow.context: In this step, you link the game to a real tool, the periscope.
flow.think: A periscope has two mirrors that turn the beam twice. Which two squares of your maze would make a periscope?

experiments.title: Where Does the Bounce Go? Mirror, foil, paper, cloth and glossy page
experiments.question: A thin beam of torchlight lands on a surface. From how many places around the surface can you see the lit spot, and does it depend on what the surface is?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which surface will show the lit spot from the most places? Which from the fewest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The torch, the card with the small hole, the angle of the beam and the distance stay the same every time. The torch is always at the same mark, 40 centimetres from the surface. Only the surface changes. You look from the same five marks each time, and you do each surface twice, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: Which of the 5 marks could you see a lit spot from?
What it looked like: sharp bright flash, even glow, faint or almost nothing

materials.item: a phone torch or small torch, and a card about 10 centimetres square with a round hole about 1 centimetre wide in the middle
a small flat mirror (a pocket or compact mirror from a general store, about Rs 20 to 40; plastic is safest) with its edges taped
5 squares about 8 centimetres wide: smooth kitchen foil with the shiny side out, crumpled foil flattened out a little, white paper, black cloth and a glossy magazine page
a big sheet of paper, about 90 centimetres wide and 45 centimetres tall (two chart papers taped side by side), and a protractor
modelling clay or a stack of books to hold each square upright, and a pencil
a room that can be made very dark, such as one with curtains closed in the evening

experiments.safety: Never look straight into the torch or its bright flash in the mirror. Glance for a moment only, from the side. A grown-up tapes the mirror's edges and draws the marks.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the surface in the middle and the five marks around it, and colour the marks that saw a lit spot. Do one drawing for the mirror and one for the white paper.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you shine a thin torch beam at six different surfaces. You find out from how many places around each surface you can see the lit spot, and what that shows about smooth and rough surfaces.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: marks (out of 5) from which the lit spot could be seen
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be a little different.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper on a table with a small dot in the middle and a half circle drawn round it, with five marks numbered 1 to 5 on the arc and a sixth mark where the torch stands.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the half circle. Mark the torch spot and five viewing marks.

setup.art: A flat mirror standing upright on the middle dot, with a torch at its mark shining a thin beam at it through a card with a small hole.
setup.caption: 2. Stand the first surface upright on the middle dot. Aim the torch at it.

setup.art: A child lying with chin on the table, looking at the mirror from mark 4, with a bright flash of reflected torch light.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the surface from each mark in turn, with your chin on the table.

setup.art: The same child looking at a white paper square from marks 1 and 5, with an even soft glow on the paper.
setup.caption: 4. Change the surface, and look from the same five marks again.

flow.do: Show your child the six surfaces and the torch. Ask which will show a lit spot from the most places and which from the fewest. Ask for reasons. Write the guesses on the table. Roles: with one child, the parent holds the torch and the child looks and writes. With 2 to 4 children, one holds the torch and one writes the table. The others each lie at a different mark. They call out together if they see the spot. Then swap places.
flow.say: A thin beam of light will land on each of these. We will look at the spot from five different places. Which surface will let you see it from the most places? Which from the fewest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A torch beam lands on six surfaces. Which shows the spot from the most places? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think a mirror will be different from paper?
good: A mirror bounces light in one direction.
Paper is rough and spreads the light.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think the mirror will show the spot from the most places because it is the shiniest. That is a very good guess to test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Where Does the Bounce Go test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up draws a dot in the middle of the big sheet. Use a string 40 centimetres long to draw a half circle round it. Use a protractor to mark the torch spot at 45 degrees from the left end of the line through the dot. Mark five viewing marks at 15, 75, 105, 135 and 165 degrees. Number them 1 to 5.
flow.say: The dot in the middle is where each surface will stand. The torch goes at its mark. We will look at the surface from five marks around the half circle.
flow.kid: Draw a dot and a half circle. Mark the torch spot and five viewing marks.
flow.parent: Measure the angles from the left end of the straight line through the dot. The torch mark is at 45 degrees. The five viewing marks are at 15, 75, 105, 135 and 165 degrees, so the mirror bounce lands on mark 4. Use a ruler or string to make sure each mark is 40 centimetres from the dot. If you lack a protractor, trace one from a maths box.

check.q: Why must the torch stay at the same mark for every surface?
options: So that only the surface changes
So that the torch looks tidy
So that the torch never runs out of battery
So that the marks are in order
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the torch moved, any difference could come from the torch's position and not from the surface. Picking 'so the torch looks tidy' mixes up neat with fair.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the marks. Everything you fix here stays the same during the test.

flow.do: Make the room dark. Stand the mirror upright on the dot with clay, facing the viewing marks. Switch on the torch at its mark, aimed at the dot through the card with the hole. Put your chin on the table at mark 1. Look at the mirror. Move to marks 2, 3, 4 and 5 in turn. Write which marks show a lit spot.
flow.say: Chin on the table. Look at the mirror from mark 1. Can you see the lit spot? Now mark 2. Keep going to mark 5. Where does the bright flash appear?
flow.kid: Put your chin on the table. Look at the mirror from each mark. Where do you see the spot?
flow.parent: Expected: a bright flash of the torch itself at mark 4, and almost nothing at the other marks. The flash can be dazzling, so glance for a moment only. A thin beam makes no visible spot on a clean mirror from any other mark. Then test the smooth foil in the same way. It should act like a weaker mirror. The mirror must lie along the straight line through the dot, so its flat faces point toward marks 1 and 5. If nobody sees the flash, nudge the mirror a little.
flow.context: In this step, you test the mirror and the smooth foil from five places.

flow.do: Swap in the crumpled foil, then the white paper, the black cloth and the glossy page, one at a time. For each, look from marks 1 to 5. Write which marks show a lit spot, and what it looks like. Repeat each surface once.
flow.say: Change the surface. Look from all five marks. Can you see the lit spot from every mark? How bright is it? Is it the same from each mark?
flow.kid: Swap the surface. Look from all five marks. Write where you see the spot.
flow.parent: Expected: the crumpled foil sparkles from most marks. White paper shows an even glow from all five marks. Black cloth shows only a faint glow, mostly from nearby marks. The glossy page shows an even glow from all marks, plus an extra bright flash at mark 4. If your results differ, write them down as they are. If the black cloth shows nothing from any mark, write 0 and say so. A brighter torch, used for every surface, helps. Do not change the distance for one surface only.

check.q: You can see the lit spot on the white paper from all five marks, but on the mirror from only one. What is the best reason?
options: Paper scatters the light in every direction, and the mirror sends it in one direction
Paper makes its own light
The mirror takes in the light
Paper is closer to the torch
check.why: The bumps in paper face every way, so the beam is scattered, and some reaches every mark. The mirror is smooth, so the beam leaves in one direction only, toward mark 4. Picking 'the mirror takes in the light' is wrong, because the mirror sends a bright flash toward mark 4.

flow.context: In this step, you test the other four surfaces from the same five marks.

flow.do: Look at your table. Sort the surfaces by how many marks saw a lit spot. Ask your child what the surfaces with the most marks have in common, and what the mirror does differently.
flow.say: The mirror showed the spot from one mark. The paper showed it from five. The same torch, the same beam. What is different about the surfaces?
flow.kid: Sort the surfaces by how many marks saw the spot. What is different about the mirror?

ask.q: Did the white paper bounce the light, or soak it up?
good: It bounced it, in every direction.
It bounced it, because we could see the spot.

flow.parent: The key idea is that the paper reflects too. We see the lit spot on the paper only because paper reflects light into our eyes, from every direction. The mirror sends all of its light in one direction. They follow the same rule, but the bumps in paper face every way.
flow.context: In this step, you work out what the results say about smooth and rough surfaces.

experiments.title: Make a Dull Thing Shine: how does polish work?
experiments.question: Four strips of the same dull black paper are treated in different ways: left alone, wiped with a damp cloth, rubbed with wax and polished, and covered with clear tape. Which one shows the sharpest reflection of a torch, and which shows the fuzziest?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which strip will show the sharpest reflection of the torch, and which the fuzziest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The four strips are cut from the same sheet of black paper. The torch, the distance and the height of your eye stay the same. You look at each strip in the same way, from the same place. Only the treatment changes. The untouched strip is the control.
results_table: Reflection of the torch when I look from a low angle: sharp, fuzzy or none
Reflection when I look from a high angle: sharp, fuzzy or none

materials.item: 4 strips of black chart paper, each 10 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide, cut from the same sheet
a white candle stub or wax crayon, unlit, about 5 centimetres long
a soft clean cloth and a small bowl of water
clear sticky tape or packing tape, about 4 centimetres wide (if your tape is narrower, press two or three pieces side by side with no gaps)
a phone torch or small torch
a ruler, a pencil and four small bits of paper to label the strips A, B, C and D

experiments.safety: Do not light the candle. Use it only as a block of wax. A grown-up supervises the water and the scissors.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the four strips in a row, with a picture of the torch's reflection on each. Write which treatment made the strip shine most.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you treat four strips of dull paper in four ways and look at the reflection of a torch in each. You find out what polish, water and tape do to a dull surface.

setup.art: Four strips of black paper in a row on a table, labelled A, B, C and D, with a candle stub, a damp cloth and a roll of clear tape beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut four strips and label them A, B, C and D.

setup.art: A hand rubbing a white candle stub hard along strip C, and then polishing it with a soft cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Rub strip C with wax and polish it. Wipe B with a damp cloth. Cover D with tape.

setup.art: A child with chin on the table looking across strip C at a torch standing 40 centimetres away, where a bright smear of light shows on the strip.
setup.caption: 3. Look across each strip from a low angle and judge the reflection of the torch.

setup.art: The same child with the head raised, looking down at the strips from a high angle, where only the taped strip shows a reflection.
setup.caption: 4. Raise your head and look down. Which strips still show a reflection?

flow.do: Show your child the four strips and what will be done to each. Ask which will shine most and which least. Write the guesses and reasons. With 2 to 4 children, each makes and judges their own set of four strips, then you compare scores. With one child, the parent is the second judge.
flow.say: Strip A we leave alone. Strip B gets wiped with a wet cloth. Strip C gets rubbed with wax and polished. Strip D gets covered with clear tape. Which will show the best reflection of a torch? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four strips of dull paper, four treatments. Which will shine best? Why?

ask.q: Why might wax or tape make paper shine?
good: They make a shiny layer on top.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think water will be best because wet things look shiny. Test it. Wet paper wrinkles, and the water soaks in, so it may help less than they expect.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Make a Dull Thing Shine test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Label the strips A, B, C and D. Leave A alone. Wipe B once with a damp cloth that is not dripping. Rub C hard with the wax block in one direction for one minute. Then polish C with a dry cloth. Smooth a strip of clear tape over D, with no bubbles.
flow.say: A is our control. We do nothing to it. B gets one wipe of damp cloth. C gets a minute of rubbing with wax, and then polishing. D gets clear tape, pressed down smooth.
flow.kid: Leave A alone. Wipe B. Rub C with wax and polish. Cover D with tape.
flow.parent: Press the tape down from one end to the other with your thumb so that no bubbles are trapped. Rub the wax in one direction only. The wax leaves a thin film that you polish with the cloth. Test strip B quickly, before it dries or wrinkles.

check.q: Why do we leave strip A alone?
options: So we can compare the treated strips with an untreated one
So we have a spare strip
Because it is already the shiniest
To save the wax
check.why: Strip A is the control. It shows what dull paper looks like with no treatment, so you can see how much each treatment changes it. Picking 'it is already the shiniest' does not fit, because it is the plain dull paper.

flow.context: In this step, you prepare the four strips.

flow.do: Dim the room. Stand the torch on the table 40 centimetres from a strip, shining along the table. Lay strip A flat in front of you. Put your chin on the table and look across the strip toward the torch. Sit on the far side of the strip so the torch is straight ahead beyond it. Score each strip. Give 0 for none, 1 for a faint smear, 2 for fuzzy but clear, and 3 for a sharp torch shape. Write what the torch's reflection looks like. Repeat for B, C and D.
flow.say: Chin on the table, looking across the strip at the torch. Can you see the torch's reflection in the strip? Is it sharp, or is it a fuzzy smear? Write it down. Then the next strip.
flow.kid: Put your chin on the table. Look across each strip at the torch. Is the reflection sharp or fuzzy?
flow.parent: Expected: A shows a faint fuzzy smear. D, the taped strip, shows the sharpest reflection of the torch. C is usually better than A. B varies, and may be no better than A. If B looks as good as D, write that down. Do not look directly at the torch. If every strip looks the same, darken the room and lower your chin until it touches the table. The effect needs a very low angle.
flow.context: In this step, you look across each strip at a low angle and judge its reflection.

flow.do: Now raise your head until you are looking down at each strip from about 30 centimetres above it. Look at each one again. Write whether the torch's reflection is sharp, fuzzy or gone. Then explain what the low angle did.
flow.say: Now look down at the strips from above. Which strips still show the torch? Which have lost it? What did lowering your head do?
flow.kid: Raise your head. Look down at each strip. Which still show the torch?

check.q: Strip A showed a faint reflection from a low angle and none from a high angle. What does this suggest?
options: Even a dull surface acts more like a mirror when you look at it from a low angle
Strip A makes its own light
Strip A is a mirror
The torch was switched off
check.why: At a very low angle, the light skims over the tiny bumps instead of hitting them head on, so the surface reflects more in order. Seen from above, the same bumps scatter the light. Picking 'strip A is a mirror' is wrong. It was dull from above.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the strips from a high angle and compare with the low angle.

experiments.title: Send It Straight Back: two mirrors at a right angle
experiments.question: A thin beam of light hits two mirrors set at a right angle. Where does it come out, and does the answer change when the beam comes in at a different angle?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After bouncing off both mirrors, will the beam come out going the same way it went in, the opposite way, or somewhere else? Will it change when the beam arrives at a different angle? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The two mirrors stay fixed in the same place at a right angle. The slit torch lies flat on the paper each time. Only the angle of the beam changes. You try three angles, and then repeat with one mirror alone for comparison.
results_table: With two mirrors: did the beam leave parallel to the way it came in?
With one mirror alone: did the beam leave parallel to the way it came in?

materials.item: 2 small flat mirrors, each at least 8 centimetres long (pocket mirrors from a general store, about Rs 20 to 40 each; plastic is safest), with edges taped
a torch lying flat, with a card taped over it with a thin slit about 2 millimetres wide, so it makes a thin line of light
a big sheet of white paper, a pencil, a ruler and a protractor
a book or a box with a square corner, to set the mirrors at a right angle
reflective tape or a reflective strip, such as from a school bag, a bicycle reflector (about Rs 20 at a cycle shop) or a safety jacket
modelling clay to hold the mirrors upright, and a room that can be made very dark

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the slit and tapes the edges of the mirrors. Never shine a torch into anyone's eyes.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the two mirrors and your three beams on the paper, with arrows to show the way in and the way out. Colour each in and out pair with the same colour.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you set two mirrors at a right angle and follow a beam through them. You find out why a bicycle reflector sends light straight back to a car's headlight.

setup.art: Two small mirrors standing upright on a sheet of paper, touching at one end and forming a right angle, with the corner of a book fitted between them.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the two mirrors at a right angle, using the corner of a book.

setup.art: A slit torch lying flat on the paper, sending a thin line of light into the mirror corner, with pencil dots marking where the line goes in.
setup.caption: 2. Shine the thin beam into the corner. Mark two dots on the beam going in.

setup.art: The same paper with two dots on the beam coming out of the corner, and a ruler joining them to make a line parallel to the way in.
setup.caption: 3. Mark two dots on the beam coming out. Join the dots with a ruler.

setup.art: A child shining a torch at a reflective strip on a school bag and seeing it glow brightly with the torch held beside the eye.
setup.caption: 4. Shine the torch at a reflective strip. Look from beside the torch.

flow.do: Show your child the two mirrors, the slit torch and the reflective strip. Ask where the beam will go after bouncing off both mirrors. Write the guess and reason. Roles: one child holds the torch, one holds the mirrors steady, one marks the dots. With one child, the parent holds the mirrors and the child marks the dots. With 4 children, two pairs can each build a corner and compare.
flow.say: Two mirrors make a corner, like the inside of an open book. A thin beam goes into the corner. It bounces off one mirror, and then the other. Which way will it come out? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two mirrors make a corner. A beam goes in. Which way will it come out? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the beam will come out that way?
good: It bounces off each mirror once.
It will go off to the side.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The beam bounces twice, once on each mirror, and each bounce follows the rule that the angle out equals the angle in.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Send It Straight Back test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Draw a line on the paper. Stand the two mirrors upright with clay, so they meet at a corner on the line, at a right angle. Use the corner of a book to check the angle. The shiny sides face each other.
flow.say: Like an open book standing up, with the shiny sides facing in. The corner of the book checks that the angle between the mirrors is a right angle.
flow.kid: Stand the mirrors like an open book. Check the corner with a book. Shiny sides in.
flow.parent: Press the clay firmly. The mirrors must not wobble. If the room is bright, close the curtains. The thin line of light is faint and needs a dark room. If the line is too faint, make the slit a little wider. To make the thin line: tape the slit card flat over the torch lamp. For a sharper line, stand a second slit card on the paper about 5 centimetres in front of the torch, and let the beam skim along the paper.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the two mirrors at a right angle.

flow.do: Lay the torch flat on the paper, aimed at the corner at about 20 degrees to the first mirror. Mark two dots on the thin line going in. Mark two dots on the line coming out. Join the dots with a ruler. Repeat at about 45 degrees and 70 degrees. Then remove one mirror and try again with one mirror alone. Use the protractor to measure the angle between each pair of lines. It should be close to 0 degrees.
flow.say: Lay the torch down. Mark two dots on the beam going in. Mark two dots on the beam coming out. Join each pair with a ruler. How do the two lines compare? Do the same for a different angle.
flow.kid: Mark the beam going in. Mark the beam coming out. Join the dots. How do the lines compare?
flow.parent: Expected: with two mirrors at a right angle, the line out is parallel to the line in, and goes back the way it came, at all three angles. With one mirror alone, the beam goes off in a different direction every time. Tiny errors are normal. Check that the lines look parallel, not that they match exactly.

check.q: With two mirrors at a right angle, the beam came out parallel to the way it went in, at all three angles. What does this show?
options: Two right-angle mirrors send light back the way it came, whatever the angle
The mirrors made the beam stronger
The torch was too bright
Light always goes parallel to everything
check.why: The first mirror turns the beam through some angle, and the second mirror turns it through exactly the opposite amount, because the mirrors are at a right angle. The beam ends up going parallel to its path in, but the other way. Picking 'the mirrors made the beam stronger' is wrong, because a mirror cannot add light.

flow.context: In this step, you follow the beam through the two mirrors at three different angles.

flow.do: Put the reflective strip on a wall or bag. Make the room dark. Shine the torch at it from different angles. Hold the torch right beside your eye and look at the strip. Then step to the side, away from the torch, and look again. Try the same with a plain white paper.
flow.say: Shine the torch on the reflective strip. Hold it right beside your eye. What do you see? Now step aside and look from there. What changes? Try plain white paper too.
flow.kid: Shine a torch at the strip. Look from beside the torch. Then step aside. What changes?
flow.parent: Expected: the reflective strip glows brightly when you look from beside the torch, from almost any angle, and looks much dimmer from the side. White paper looks equally lit from both places. The strip is built from many tiny corner mirrors, or from tiny glass beads, which send light back toward the torch.
flow.context: In this step, you test a reflective strip, which works like many tiny pairs of mirrors.

activities.title: Shiny or Dull Hunt: twelve things and the window test

materials.item: 12 things from the home: a steel tumbler, a steel spoon, flat kitchen foil, crumpled foil, white paper, a glossy magazine page, a black cloth, a brass lamp or bell, a floor tile, a wooden door or table, a coin and a smooth stone
a window with bright daylight, or a lamp
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess, run the window test on twelve things, look from a low angle, and sort the results.

activities.record: A table with twelve things, your guess for each, what you saw in each one (clear window, fuzzy window or none), and a final sort into three piles.
activities.safety: Never look at the Sun, or at its reflection in any shiny thing. Test with the window behind you, in daylight that is not direct sun, or use a lamp.
activities.context: In this activity, you test twelve things around your home to see which show a clear image of a window, which show a blur, and which show nothing. You find out what the shiny ones have in common.

setup.art: Twelve household things laid in a row on a table near a bright window, from a steel tumbler to a black cloth.
setup.caption: 1. Line up the twelve things. Guess which will show the window.

setup.art: A child holding a steel tumbler up in front of a window and looking for the window shape in it.
setup.caption: 2. Hold each thing up. Can you see the window in it?

setup.art: A child with chin on a table looking across a plain wooden table at a window, where a bright patch of the window shows.
setup.caption: 3. Try the low angle. Look across each thing from table level.

flow.do: Line up the twelve things on a table near the window. Ask your child to guess for each one whether it will show the window clearly, fuzzily or not at all. Write the guesses in a table. With 2 to 4 children, share the twelve things out. Each child guesses and tests their own. Then check each other's results.
flow.say: Look at each thing. If we hold it up to the window, will we see the window in it? Clearly, fuzzily or not at all? Write down your guess for each one.
flow.kid: Look at twelve things. Guess which show the window. Write your guesses.

ask.q: Which is the hardest to guess?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Any guess is fine. The foil, tile and stone are good surprises.
flow.context: This is the first step of Shiny or Dull Hunt. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Test each thing in turn. Hold it up, with the window or lamp behind you, and look for the window shape in it. Write down clear, fuzzy or none. Look at the steel tumbler, spoon and foil from different angles.
flow.say: Stand with the window behind you. Hold up each thing and look for the shape of the window in it. Can you see the panes and the frame? Clearly, fuzzily or not at all?
flow.kid: Hold each thing up. Look for the window in it. Clear, fuzzy or none?
flow.parent: Expected: the tumbler, spoon, flat foil and tile show the window clearly or almost. The coin, brass lamp, magazine page and wood show a fuzzy or partial one. White paper, black cloth and crumpled foil show nothing clear. Stone depends on how smooth it is. Write what you see.

check.q: Crumpled foil is shiny, but shows no clear window. Why?
options: Its many little folds face every way and scatter the light
Foil makes its own light
Crumpled foil is too thin
It only works in sunlight
check.why: Each flat fold of the foil is a tiny mirror, but each one faces a different way. The rays leave in every direction, so no clear window forms. Picking 'foil makes its own light' mixes up shining with making light.

flow.context: In this step, you do the window test on each of the twelve things.

flow.do: Put your chin on the table beside the wooden table, the tile and the paper. Look across each one toward the window or lamp. Write whether you see a bright reflection of it at this low angle.
flow.say: Put your chin down. Look across the table toward the window. Can you see a bright patch where the window is reflected? Now the paper. Now the tile.
flow.kid: Put your chin on the table. Look across the wood, the tile and the paper. Do you see the window?
flow.parent: At a low angle, even dull things show a bright reflection. Wood, paper and tile are good ones to try. This is why a wet road glares at night. The light skims over the bumps.
flow.context: In this step, you look at surfaces from a very low angle and see them act like mirrors.

flow.do: Sort the twelve things into three piles: clear, fuzzy and none. Ask what the things in the clear pile have in common.
flow.say: Make three piles. What do the things in the clear pile have in common? What about the none pile?
flow.kid: Sort into three piles. What do the clear ones have in common?
flow.context: In this step, you sort what you found and look for what the shiny things share.

activities.title: Colour Bounce: a white page catches the colour next to it

materials.item: a sheet of white paper and a sheet of white card
2 sheets of bright coloured chart paper: red and green, or red and blue
a bright torch or phone torch, or a sunny window
a book or a box to stand the card on

schedule.what: Stand a red card beside a white one, shine light on the red, and see whether the white picks up a tint.

activities.record: Draw the two cards side by side, and colour the white card where it picked up a tint. Write what you saw with red, green and no coloured card.
activities.context: In this activity, you stand a bright red card next to a white one, and light the red one. You find out that light bounces off one surface onto another, and carries its colour with it.

setup.art: A red card and a white card standing in a V shape like a half-open book on a table in a dim room, with a torch shining only on the red card.
setup.caption: 1. Stand a red and a white card in a V. Shine the torch on the red one only.

setup.art: A close view of the white card with a faint pink glow near the fold where it meets the red card.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the white card near the fold. Does it look pink?

setup.art: The same cards with the red replaced by green, and a faint green glow on the white card.
setup.caption: 3. Swap the red for green. What colour does the white card take?

flow.do: Show your child the red card and the white card. Ask what will happen to the white card if you shine a torch on the red card only. Ask for a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: We stand a red card next to a white card. We shine the torch only on the red card. Will the white card change? How? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A red card next to a white card. Light only the red one. Will the white card change? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the white card might change colour?
good: The red light might bounce onto it.
It might not change at all.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Colour Bounce. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Make the room dim. Fold the white card and the red card into a V, like a half-open book, with about a right angle between them. Stand them on the table. Shine the torch at the red card, so the beam hits only the red. Look at the white card near the fold. Shine the torch from about 15 centimetres, at a slant along the red card. No direct light may fall on the white card. Hold the plain white paper well away from the red and compare its colour with the white card near the fold. Give the tint a score from 0 (none) to 3 (clear) at the fold, 5 centimetres from it and 10 centimetres from it. With 2 to 4 children, one holds the torch, one holds the cards, and the others score.
flow.say: The beam lands only on the red card. Look at the white card, close to the fold. Do you see any colour on it? Move your eyes further from the fold. What happens?
flow.kid: Light only the red card. Look at the white card near the fold. Do you see any colour?
flow.parent: Expected: a faint pink glow on the white card near the fold, that fades further away. The effect is subtle. A very dim room and a bright torch help. If you cannot see it, hold a clean sheet of white paper beside the white card for comparison. It will look plainer. The most reliable way is a sunny window: lay the red card in bright daylight beside the white card, with no direct sun on the white. Never look into the sun.

check.q: The torch light only landed on the red card, yet the white card looked slightly pink near the fold. Why?
options: Light bounced off the red card onto the white card, carrying red with it
The white card made its own pink light
The torch was pink
White paper turns pink in the dark
check.why: The red card mostly scatters red light and absorbs the other colours. Some of that red light lands on the white card and scatters again, into your eyes. So the white card looks slightly pink where it catches the red light. Picking 'the torch was pink' does not fit, because the same torch makes the white card look plain when the red card is removed.

flow.context: In this step, you look for a tint on a white card, from light that bounced off a red card.

flow.do: Swap the red for the green card, and shine the torch on the green only. Look at the white card. Then take the coloured card away and shine the torch at the white one alone. Compare.
flow.say: Now the green card. What colour does the white card take? Now take the green away. What does the white card look like by itself?
flow.kid: Swap in the green card. Light it. What colour does the white card take?
flow.parent: The white card should pick up a green tint near the fold, and none when the coloured card is removed. This is the same reason a person standing beside a bright red wall looks slightly flushed.
flow.context: In this step, you swap the red card for a green one and compare.

flow.do: Talk about where you see this at home. Sunlight on a green wall can turn a white ceiling slightly green. A yellow wall can make a room glow warm.
flow.say: Where might this happen at home? A bright curtain in the sun, a coloured wall, a red cloth near a white sheet. Have you ever seen a white thing look tinted?
flow.kid: Where could a bright wall tint a white thing at home?
flow.context: In this step, you look for where the same thing happens at home.

activities.title: Steel Katori Beam: a bowl that gathers light and a back that spreads it

materials.item: a polished steel katori or a large steel spoon
a torch (a phone torch is fine), propped on books about 2 metres away and aimed at the katori
a white card, about 15 centimetres square
a room that can be made dark

schedule.what: Aim a torch beam from across the room at the inside of a bowl and at its back, and catch the light on a white card.

activities.record: Draw the torch, the katori and the card. Show where the bright spot was smallest. Write what the back of the katori did to the beam.
activities.safety: Use a torch only, never sunlight. A curved mirror can focus sunlight into a spot hot enough to burn skin or start a fire, and can harm eyes. Never look into the bright reflection.
activities.context: In this activity, you aim a torch at the inside and outside of a steel katori and catch the reflected light on a card. You find out how curved mirrors gather and spread light.

setup.art: A steel katori standing on its side on a table with a torch shining into the bowl and a white card catching the reflected light.
setup.caption: 1. Shine the torch into the inside of the katori. Hold the white card to catch the light.

setup.art: A small bright spot of light on the white card, with a ruler showing the distance from the katori.
setup.caption: 2. Move the card until the spot is smallest and brightest.

setup.art: The same katori turned around so that the back faces the torch, with a large dim patch of light on the white card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the katori round. Shine the torch on its back. What does the card show?

flow.do: Show your child the katori. Ask what a torch beam will do after bouncing off the inside of the bowl, and off the outside. Ask for guesses and reasons. Write them.
flow.say: The inside of the katori curves in. The back curves out. If we shine a torch on each, will the light look different on a card? How? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A torch shines on the inside of a bowl and on its back. Will the light look different? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the bowl will change the beam?
good: It curves, so it bends the light.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Steel Katori Beam. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Make the room dark. Prop the torch on books about 2 metres away, aimed at you. Hold the katori with its inside facing the torch, tilted a little so the reflected light goes off to one side. Hold the white card in that reflected light, a few centimetres from the bowl. Move it back and forth until the spot is smallest and brightest. Measure the distance from the bowl to the card.
flow.say: Aim the torch into the bowl. Hold the card to catch the light that comes back. Slide the card nearer and further. Where is the spot smallest and brightest?
flow.kid: Aim the torch into the bowl. Catch the light on the card. Find the smallest spot.
flow.parent: With one child, the parent props the torch and the child holds the katori and card. With 2 to 4 children, one holds the katori, one holds the card, one measures, then swap. Do not look into the bowl at the beam. The bright spot forms a few centimetres in front of a small katori, at the focus. A katori is deep, so the spot is a soft blob, not a point. If you cannot find it, tilt the katori more and move the card slowly.

check.q: The inside of the katori made the light into a small, bright spot. What does a concave mirror do?
options: It gathers light to a point
It makes new light
It spreads light in every direction
It absorbs light
check.why: The curve of the inside tilts every tiny patch so that the reflected rays cross at one spot. The light there is packed tight, so it is bright. Picking 'it spreads light' describes the outside of the bowl, not the inside.

flow.context: In this step, you find the focus of the bowl, the place where it gathers the light.

flow.do: Turn the katori round, so that its back faces the torch. Catch the light on the card and move the card as before. Compare it with the inside. Then light the room. Look at your face in the inside of a large steel spoon, at arm's length. Look in the back too.
flow.say: Now the back of the katori. Where does the light go? Is it small and bright, or large and dim? What is different from before?
flow.kid: Turn the katori round. Shine the torch on its back. Is the spot big or small?
flow.parent: The back spreads the beam into a wide, dim patch with no sharp spot. That is why convex mirrors, which curve outward, are used on cars and in shop corners: they show a wide view. This is a good moment to name the two kinds, concave and convex. Expected: the back never makes a small bright spot, only a dim wide patch. In the inside of the spoon your face is usually upside down; in the back it is upright and small.
flow.context: In this step, you compare the back of the katori with the inside.

activities.title: Dusk Reflector Hunt: what glows back at a torch?

materials.item: a torch
a grown-up to come along
a notebook and a pencil
a safe place to walk at dusk, such as a quiet street, a school path or an apartment car park

schedule.what: Walk at dusk with a torch and find things that glow back. Compare them with dull things.

activities.record: A list of at least six things that glowed back at the torch, and three that did not, with a note on where you were standing when each glowed.
activities.safety: A grown-up must come. Stay on the pavement or in a safe space, away from traffic. Never shine a torch into a driver's eyes or at people.
activities.context: In this activity, you walk at dusk with a torch and look for things that glow back at you. You find out how reflectors work and why they are on bicycles, vehicles and road signs.

setup.art: A child with a torch held beside their eye, shining at a bicycle reflector that glows bright red.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the torch beside your eye. Shine it at a reflector.

setup.art: A road sign and a painted wall side by side at dusk, with a torch beam lighting both, and only the sign glowing.
setup.caption: 2. Compare a reflective sign with a painted wall.

setup.art: A child stepping to one side and looking at the same reflector, which now looks dim.
setup.caption: 3. Step to the side. Does the glow stay?

flow.do: Before you go out, ask your child to guess what kinds of things will glow back at a torch. Write the guesses. Check the torch works. With 2 to 4 children, give each their own torch and a job: spotter, recorder, side-stepper. One grown-up can look after up to four children on a quiet path.
flow.say: We will walk at dusk with a torch. What kinds of things do you think will glow back at us when we shine the torch on them? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Walk at dusk with a torch. What kinds of things will glow back? Why?

ask.q: What do you expect to glow back?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children expect shiny things such as mirrors, and are surprised by the reflective patches on signs, bags and clothes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dusk Reflector Hunt. You guess before you go out.

flow.do: Walk with a grown-up. Hold the torch beside your eye. Shine it at bicycle reflectors, the red patches on autos and trucks, and road signs. Try number plates, school bag stripes and cat's eyes in the road. Write down each thing that glows. Try a painted wall and a plain sign for comparison.
flow.say: Hold the torch right beside your eye. Shine it at a reflector. Does it glow? Now try a painted wall. Does it glow? Write down what you find.
flow.kid: Hold the torch beside your eye. Shine it at reflectors. Write what glows back.
flow.parent: Expected: bicycle reflectors, signs, number plates, cat's eyes and reflective stripes glow brightly. Painted walls and plain signs do not. Do not shine the torch at drivers. If there is nothing to see, look at the reflectors on your own bicycle or bag.
flow.context: In this step, you walk and find things that glow back at your torch.

flow.do: Choose one glowing reflector. Stand in front of it with the torch beside your eye and note the glow. Then step to the side, keep the torch pointing at it, and look from where you stand. Compare the two. Then step back a few paces at a time and count how many paces away you can still see the glow.
flow.say: Look at the reflector with the torch beside your eye. Now step to the side but keep the torch pointed at it. Does it glow as brightly from here?
flow.kid: Look from beside the torch. Then step to the side. Does the glow stay?

check.q: A bicycle reflector glows brightly when a car's headlight lights it, and the driver sees the glow. Why is the glow so good for the driver?
options: It sends the light straight back toward the headlight, near the driver's eyes
It makes its own light
It spreads the light evenly in every direction
It takes in the light and stores it
check.why: A reflector is made of many tiny corner mirrors that send light back the way it came. The driver's eyes are near the headlights, so the driver gets the glow. Picking 'it makes its own light' mixes up reflecting with making light. A reflector is dark when no light shines on it.

flow.context: In this step, you test how a reflector's glow depends on where you stand.

projects.title: Milk-Carton Periscope: see over the wall

materials.item: a clean, dry juice or tall box carton about 7 centimetres square and at least 19 centimetres tall (Indian milk comes in pouches, so use a 1 litre juice carton or a cereal-box sleeve, or tape stiff card into a square tube)
2 flat mirrors, each about 7 centimetres wide and 7 centimetres tall: pocket mirrors, or pieces cut by a local glass shop with the edges smoothed (about Rs 20 to 40 each), with the edges taped
2 strips of thin card, each 7 centimetres wide and 24 centimetres long, to fold into triangle wedges
sticky tape, a ruler and a pencil
scissors and a craft knife, for a grown-up to use
a black marker or black paper, to darken the inside

projects.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting with the craft knife and scissors. Tape over the edges of the mirrors, because the edges can be sharp. Glass mirrors break, so keep them away from small children and handle them over a table.

schedule.what: Prepare the carton, cut the windows, make the two wedges and stick the mirrors on them.
Fit the wedges, test the periscope, fix any problems and use it to see over a wall.

projects.record: Draw a side view of your periscope with the two mirrors, the two windows and a ray of light zigzagging through them. Write what you saw when you looked into it, and which way up the picture was.
projects.context: In this project, you build a periscope from a milk carton and two mirrors. You use it to see over a wall or round a corner, and find out why the picture stays upright.

setup.art: A milk carton with its top and bottom cut off, a window cut near the top of the front face and a window near the bottom of the back face.
setup.caption: 1. Cut the ends off the carton. Cut a window at the top front and one at the bottom back.

setup.art: A triangle wedge made from folded card with two equal short sides and a mirror taped onto the long sloping side.
setup.caption: 2. Fold a card wedge and tape a mirror onto its sloping side.

setup.art: The two wedges placed at the top and bottom of the carton so that the mirrors face each other, one tilted down and one tilted up.
setup.caption: 3. Fit the wedges at the two ends. The mirrors lean the same way and face each other.

setup.art: A child holding the periscope up beside a garden wall, looking into the lower window and seeing a bird on the far side.
setup.caption: 4. Hold the periscope above a wall, and look into the lower window.

flow.do: Show your child the carton and mirrors. Ask what they will see if they look into the lower window while holding the periscope above a wall. Ask if the picture will be the right way up. Write the guesses. With 2 to 4 children, work in pairs. One pair builds the carton and the other makes the wedges. Then join them. With one child, the parent does the cutting and the child folds, tapes and tests.
flow.say: A periscope uses two mirrors to look over a wall. What will you see through the lower window? Will the picture be upside down, back to front or the right way up? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A periscope has two mirrors. Will the picture be the right way up? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the picture will come out that way?
good: One mirror flips it, and the other flips it back.
It will be the right way up.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect the picture to be flipped or upside down. Test it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Milk-Carton Periscope project. You guess before you build.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts off the top and bottom of the carton. Cut a window 5 centimetres wide and 4 centimetres tall in the front face, starting 1 centimetre below the top edge. Turn the carton round. Cut a window of the same size in the back face, starting 1 centimetre above the bottom edge. Colour the inside black.
flow.say: The two windows must be on opposite faces. One is near the top on the front. One is near the bottom on the back. Make sure they face opposite ways.
flow.kid: Cut the ends off. Cut a window at the top front. Cut one at the bottom back.
flow.parent: Check that the carton is clean and dry. The windows must be on opposite faces, one high and one low. Colouring the inside black cuts down stray reflections and makes the picture clearer.
flow.context: In this step, you prepare the carton and cut the two windows.

flow.do: Take a card strip. Fold it at 7 centimetres and at 14 centimetres, so the three sides are 7, 7 and about 10 centimetres. Check that the corner between the two 7 centimetre sides is a right angle. Tape the ends together to make a triangle tube. Tape a mirror onto the long side, shiny side out. Make the second wedge the same way.
flow.say: We make two wedges, each a triangle with two short sides and one long side. The mirror goes on the long side, shiny side out. Use the corner of a book to check the right angle.
flow.kid: Fold a card strip into a triangle. Tape a mirror on the long side. Make two.
flow.parent: The triangle with sides 7, 7 and 10 centimetres has a right angle between its two short sides and a 45 degree slope on its long side. That slope is what turns the light through a right angle. If you have no mirrors, glue smooth kitchen foil flat onto the card. The picture will be wobbly but visible. Try the wedge in the carton before taping. Cartons are a little narrower than 7 centimetres inside, so if a wedge is too tight, trim 2 or 3 millimetres off its sides.

check.q: Why is the long side of each wedge set at 45 degrees?
options: A mirror at 45 degrees turns a ray through a right angle
It makes the periscope taller
It makes the mirrors lighter
It makes the picture bigger
check.why: A ray that hits a mirror tilted at 45 degrees leaves at a right angle to the way it came in. Light going straight in turns down the tube, and later turns out again. Picking 'bigger' is a common idea, but a flat mirror does not change the size of a picture.

flow.context: In this step, you make the two wedges that hold the mirrors at exactly 45 degrees.

flow.do: On day 2, slide one wedge into the top of the carton. Its top leg lies along the top edge. Its flat leg lies against the back wall. Its mirror faces the front window. Slide the second wedge into the bottom. Its flat leg lies against the front wall, and its mirror faces the back window. Tape both in place. Look into the lower window.
flow.say: Top wedge: the mirror faces down and toward the front window. Bottom wedge: the mirror faces up and toward the back window. Both mirrors lean the same way, with their shiny sides facing each other.
flow.kid: Fit the top wedge. Fit the bottom wedge. The mirrors face each other. Look in the lower window.
flow.parent: If you see only black, check that the mirrors face each other and that the windows are on opposite faces. If you see a tilted picture, one wedge is crooked. Press the wedges to sit flat against the walls. The picture should come out upright and the right way round.
flow.context: In this step, you fit the two mirror wedges into the carton to make the periscope.

flow.do: Hold the periscope up beside a wall, a sofa or a door, with the top window facing the far side. Look into the lower window. Write what you see. Test whether writing, such as a word on a page, looks the right way round. Measure how much higher the top window is than the lower one. Find something that height to see over.
flow.say: Hold the periscope above the wall with the top window facing the far side. Look in the lower window. What do you see? Is the picture the right way up? Can you read a word held up in front of the top window?
flow.kid: Hold the periscope up. Look in the lower window. What do you see? Is it the right way up?

ask.q: Why does the picture come out the right way up?
good: The first mirror flips it and the second flips it back.
The two mirrors cancel each other.

flow.parent: The first mirror flips the picture, and the second flips it back. The two flips cancel, so the picture is upright and not reversed. Writing held in front of the top window reads the right way round. A 19 centimetre periscope lifts your eye by only about 12 to 14 centimetres. That is enough to see over a sofa arm, a box or a low wall, not a tall wall. For a taller thing, make a taller tube.
flow.context: In this step, you use the periscope and check that its picture is upright.

challenges.title: Look Round Two Corners: a bendy periscope
challenges.problem: A toy sits on the floor on the far side of a sofa, and another round a corner of the hallway. Make a periscope using three or more mirrors that lets you see the toy without moving your head from one spot.
constraints: Use only mirrors, card, tape and clay or books to hold them.
Do not move the toy, and do not move your head from the spot you chose.
You must be able to see the toy clearly.
Try it with at least three mirrors.
materials: at least 3 small flat mirrors (pocket mirrors from a general store, or plastic), with taped edges
a torch, to check the path of the light
general: A periscope with two mirrors set parallel, like the Milk-Carton Periscope, to see over the sofa.
Two mirrors, each turning the light through a right angle, one after the other.
Three mirrors in a row, each turning the path a quarter turn, to go round a corner and back.
creative: Four mirrors in a Z shape, to look round two corners.
A long cardboard tube with mirrors at each end.
Use a torch first to find the path from the toy to your eye, then place a mirror at each corner.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch the path of light from the toy to your eye, with a mirror at each turn. Build it and test it. Which design showed the toy most clearly? How many mirrors did you need, and why?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about mirrors that turn the path of light. You use three or more mirrors to see something hidden.

setup.art: A bird's-eye drawing of a room with a sofa, a hidden toy and a zigzag line of light going from the toy via three mirrors to a child's eye.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch the path from the toy to your eye, with a mirror at every turn.

setup.art: Three small mirrors on clay stands placed along a floor at different angles, with a torch beam bouncing from one to the next.
setup.caption: 2. Place the mirrors. Use a torch to check the path.

setup.art: A child looking at a mirror and seeing a toy that is hidden behind a sofa.
setup.caption: 3. Look in the first mirror. Can you see the toy?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch the path of the light from the toy to their eye, and mark where each mirror goes. With 2 to 4 children, each sketches a path first and then you pick one to build together. With one child, the parent holds mirrors while the child adjusts.
flow.say: The light from the toy must get to your eye. Draw its path as straight lines. Wherever the line turns, there must be a mirror. How many turns do you need?
flow.kid: Draw the path from the toy to your eye. A mirror goes at each turn.

ask.q: How do you know where to put each mirror?
good: At every corner of the light's path.
I put it where the light needs to go next.

flow.context: This is the first step of Look Round Two Corners. You plan.

flow.do: Place the mirrors and test them. Start by shining the torch from your eye position and follow the beam from mirror to mirror to the toy. Adjust each mirror by a small amount at a time.
flow.say: Start from your eye. Shine the torch along the path. Does the beam reach the toy? Adjust the nearest mirror a little. Then the next.
flow.kid: Place the mirrors. Shine the torch along the path. Adjust each mirror a little.
flow.parent: Light is reversible. If the torch's beam can go from your eye to the toy, the toy's light can go back to your eye. Tiny changes of angle move the beam a lot, so adjust slowly. Work in a dim room so the beam shows on the walls.
flow.context: In this step, you place and adjust the mirrors, using a torch to find the path.

flow.do: When you can see the toy, count the mirrors you used. Ask how a different layout might need fewer. Draw the final path.
flow.say: You can see the toy. How many mirrors did you use? Could you have used fewer? Draw the path the light takes.
flow.kid: Count the mirrors you used. Could you use fewer? Draw the path.

check.q: Your bendy periscope shows the toy. Which statement fits best?
options: Each mirror turns the path, and an even number of mirrors keeps the picture the right way round
More mirrors always make the picture brighter
The mirrors make the toy bigger
Mirrors turn the picture upside down
check.why: Each flat mirror flips the picture front to back once. An even number of flips cancels out, so two or four mirrors give an upright picture, while one or three give a reversed one. More mirrors make the picture slightly dimmer, because each mirror loses a little light.

flow.context: In this step, you check your design and think about what the mirrors do to the picture.

challenges.safety: Tape the edges of every mirror. Use a torch only, never sunlight.

challenges.title: Wide-View Shop Mirror: see the whole room from one spot
challenges.problem: You are a shopkeeper in a small room with a door on one side and two corners on the other. Find the shiny surface from the kitchen that lets you see the most of the room from your chair, without moving.
constraints: Test at least four different shiny things.
Place five small toys around the room: two in corners, one by the door and two on the walls.
Sit in one chair and do not move your head.
Count how many of the five toys you can see in each shiny thing.
materials: a steel katori, a large steel spoon, a steel tumbler, a flat steel plate and a ladle
general: A flat mirror or flat plate shows only a small part of the room.
The back of a spoon or the back of a katori curves outward and shows a wider view.
A convex surface shows more of the room, but everything looks smaller.
creative: Hang a steel katori by a string in a corner at the height of your eyes.
Try a steel tumbler on its side, which curves in only one direction.
Combine a flat mirror and a curved one, to see the door in one and the corner in the other.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch the room, the chair and the toys. Test each shiny thing and count the toys you can see. Which showed the most? What was the cost of the wider view? How would you improve it?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about curved mirrors. You find which shiny kitchen thing works best as a wide-view mirror.

setup.art: A bird's-eye drawing of a small room with a chair, a door and five small toys placed around the walls and corners.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the room and place the five toys.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair holding the back of a steel katori in front of their face, looking at several toys in it.
setup.caption: 2. Hold each shiny thing in front of you and count the toys you see.

setup.art: A table of results with a short bar for the flat plate and a long bar for the back of the katori.
