flow.do: Read the problem together. Place the five toys round the room. Ask your child to guess which shiny thing will show the most toys. Write the guess.
flow.say: A shopkeeper wants to see the whole shop from one chair. Which of these shiny things do you think will show the most toys? Why?
flow.kid: Which shiny thing shows the most toys? Why? Guess first.

ask.q: What shape of mirror do you think shows the widest view?

flow.context: This is the first step of Wide-View Shop Mirror. You plan and guess.

flow.do: Sit on the chair. Hold each shiny thing at arm's length in front of you. Count how many of the five toys you can see in it. Write the number. Test at least four things, and repeat each once. With 2 to 4 children, each child sits in the chair in turn and counts, and the others check the count. With one child, the parent places the toys.
flow.say: Hold the first shiny thing at arm's length. Count the toys you can see in it. Write the number. Do the same for each one.
flow.kid: Hold each shiny thing at arm's length. Count the toys you see. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Expected: the flat plate shows the fewest. The backs of the katori and the spoon, which curve outward, show the most. The steel tumbler lies in between. Things look smaller in the curved ones. Write what you find.
flow.context: In this step, you test each shiny thing and count the toys.

flow.do: Compare the numbers. Ask why the best one showed more of the room. Ask what you lose with the wide view. Try to improve your design with one change.
flow.say: Which showed the most? Why does a shape that curves outward show more of the room? What do the toys look like in it?
flow.kid: Which showed the most toys? What do the toys look like in it?

check.q: The back of the katori showed more of the room than a flat plate, but the toys looked smaller. Why?
options: A curve that bulges outward spreads the view over a wider space, so each thing is squeezed smaller
The katori is bigger than the plate
The katori makes its own light
The toys shrank
check.why: Each tiny patch of a convex mirror faces a different way, so the mirror collects light from a wide range of directions. All that is squeezed into a small picture. That is why shop mirrors and car side mirrors show a wide view where things look small.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the shiny things and explain the trade-off of a wide view.

items.p: A white wall and a mirror both reflect light. Why do you see a clear picture of your face in the mirror but not in the wall?
opts: The mirror is smooth and sends light back in order, but the wall scatters it in every direction
The mirror makes its own light
The wall takes in all the light
The wall is too big
items.why: Both bounce light. The mirror is smooth, so the rays leave together in order and your eye collects a picture. The wall is made of tiny bumps facing every way, so the rays leave in every direction. Picking 'the wall takes in all the light' is a common idea, but you can see the wall only because it reflects.

items.p: A white wall reflects no light, which is why it shows no picture of you. True or false?
items.why: False. You can see the wall only because it reflects light into your eyes. It reflects in every direction, so there is no single picture. A strong answer says the wall reflects but scatters.

items.p: When a rough surface sends light off in every direction, this is called ____ reflection.
items.why: Scattered reflection happens when the bumps face every way. The rays go off in many directions, and you can see the surface from anywhere.

items.p: Match each surface to what you see in it.
pairs: a clean bathroom mirror
a clear picture of your face
a glossy magazine page
a bright patch of the lamp and a soft picture
a white wall
no picture, but the wall looks the same from everywhere
a mirror covered in fog
no picture, because tiny drops scatter the light
items.why: Smooth surfaces make clear pictures. Partly smooth surfaces make soft ones. Rough surfaces and fog scatter the light and make none.

items.p: Sort these. Does the surface show a clear picture, or a blurry picture or none?
items: still water in a steel basin
the screen of a switched-off phone
items.why: A clear picture needs a surface so smooth that its bumps are much smaller than a wavelength of light. Cloth, clay and chalk are rough, and scatter the light.

items.p: A shoeshine man polishes a dull black shoe, and it gleams. What did the polish do?
opts: It filled and flattened the tiny bumps, so light reflects in order
It added light to the shoe
It made the shoe heavier
It made the shoe a darker colour
items.why: Polish fills the tiny dips and rubbing makes the top smooth. A smoother surface reflects in order and shows bright reflections. Picking 'it added light' mixes up shining with making light.

items.p: A rough surface breaks the rule that light leaves at the same angle at which it arrived. True or false?
items.why: False. The rule holds on every tiny flat patch of the surface. A rough surface is made of patches tilted every way, so the rays go in different directions. Nothing is broken.

items.p: Fog covers a bathroom mirror. Explain why you cannot see your face in it, even though the mirror is still there.
items.a: The fog is made of thousands of tiny drops of water. Each drop scatters light in a different direction. The smooth glass under the fog can no longer send light back in order, so no picture forms. When the fog clears, the picture returns.
items.why: A strong answer says the drops scatter the light, and that the mirror itself has not changed.

items.p: Which tool uses two mirrors so that you can see over a wall?
opts: A periscope
A magnifying glass
A pair of spectacles
A camera with a lens
items.why: A periscope has a mirror at each end of a tube. Light from the scene goes down the tube by two bounces to your eye.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to follow a ray of light through a periscope.
items: The ray enters the top window
It bounces off the top mirror and turns down the tube
It bounces off the lower mirror and turns toward the viewer
It leaves the lower window and enters the viewer's eye
items.why: The ray turns twice, once at each mirror. Each mirror is tilted at 45 degrees, so each turns the ray through a right angle.

items.p: A mirror tilted at ____ degrees turns a ray of light through a right angle.
items.why: At 45 degrees, the ray meets the mirror at 45 degrees and leaves at 45 degrees on the other side. The two angles together make a right angle.

items.p: Draw a side view of a periscope. Show the two mirrors, the two windows and the path of a ray of light from the top window to the eye.
items.a: A tall tube with a window near the top on one face and a window near the bottom on the opposite face. A mirror sloping at 45 degrees behind each window, with shiny sides facing each other. A zigzag ray enters the top window, turns down, turns again and leaves the lower window.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the mirrors parallel to each other, the windows on opposite faces, and the ray turning through a right angle at each mirror.
items.art: An empty tall rectangle drawn on a page, with no mirrors and no rays.

items.p: A bicycle reflector glows brightly when a car's headlight shines on it. What is the best reason?
opts: It sends the light back toward the headlight with many tiny corner mirrors
It makes its own light
It spreads the light evenly in every direction
It takes in the light and stores it for later
items.why: A reflector is made of many tiny corner mirrors at right angles. They send light straight back the way it came, so the driver, near the headlight, sees a bright glow. Picking 'it makes its own light' is a common idea, but a reflector is dark if no light shines on it.

items.p: On a wet road at night, the street lights make long bright streaks. Three people explain why.

views.says: The water on the road acts like a mirror, so you see the lamps in it.
The water fills the tiny bumps in the road, so it is smoother. And we see it at a low angle, which helps.
The water makes its own light when the lamps shine on it.

items.ask: Which explanation fits best with what you know about smooth surfaces and low angles? Say why, and say one thing another view gets right.
items.a: Farhan's view fits best. Water fills the bumps, making the surface smoother, and a low angle makes any surface reflect more in order. Kavya's idea is partly right, as the wet road behaves like a mirror. The uncle's idea is wrong. Water does not make light.
items.why: A strong answer picks one view with a reason from smoothness or angle, and credits a point from another view.

items.p: If you look across a plain white page from a very low angle, you can see a bright reflection of a lamp in it. True or false?
items.why: True. At a very low angle, light skims over the tiny bumps instead of hitting them, so even a dull surface reflects in order. This is why a book page or a tiled floor can show a lamp when seen from low down.

items.p: A white wall reflects 8 out of every 10 parts of the light that lands on it. If 200 units of light land on it, how many units are reflected?
items.why: 8 out of 10 is 8 tenths. A tenth of 200 is 20. 8 times 20 is 160. So 160 units are reflected and 40 are absorbed.

worksheets.title: Mirrors That Turn, Gather and Return Light (stretch)

items.p: In a periscope, the first mirror flips the picture and the second mirror flips it again. What does the viewer see?
opts: The picture upright and not reversed
The picture upside down
The picture reversed left to right
No picture
items.why: The first flip is undone by the second. Two flips cancel out. One flip alone would reverse the picture, as in a single mirror.

items.p: A black cloth reflects no light at all. True or false?
items.why: False. Black cloth reflects a small share of the light, which is why you can see its folds. Some very black materials take in more than 99.9 parts in 100 of the light, but nothing takes in all of it.

items.p: A ray of light leaves a flat mirror at the same ____ at which it arrived.
items.why: This is the rule of reflection, which you met in Class 3. It holds on every tiny flat patch of every surface.

items.p: A friend says, 'A scratched aluminium pot cannot send a signal flash, because it does not reflect sunlight.' What is wrong with this idea?
items.a: The pot does reflect sunlight. That is why it glows. But its scratches face every way, so the light is scattered in all directions instead of in one beam. A flash needs a smooth surface, so that the light goes in one direction and can be aimed.
items.why: A strong answer says the pot does reflect, and that scattering stops it from being aimed.

items.p: Match each tool to its job.
pairs: a concave mirror
gathers light to a bright spot
a convex mirror
shows a wide view, in a small size
a retroreflector
sends light straight back the way it came
a periscope
lets you see over or round something
items.why: Each tool uses the same rule of reflection. The difference is in the shape of the mirror and how many mirrors there are.

items.p: Sort these. Does the mirror curve inward, like the inside of a spoon, or outward, like the back?
items: the mirror behind a torch bulb
items.why: Inward curves gather light to a focus. Outward curves spread it out, and show a wide view.

items.p: The biggest telescopes use a curved mirror and not a big glass lens. What is the best reason?
opts: A mirror bounces all colours at the same angle, so there are no coloured fringes
A mirror is lighter than a lens
A mirror makes its own light
A mirror makes stars brighter
items.why: Glass bends different colours by different amounts, so a lens gives coloured fringes. A mirror reflects every colour alike. A big mirror is also easier to hold up and support from behind. Picking 'a mirror makes stars brighter' is wrong. It only gathers more of their light.

items.p: Two mirrors set at a right angle send a beam back parallel to its path in, whatever angle it came in at. True or false?
items.why: True. The first mirror turns the beam by some angle and the second turns it back by the opposite amount. The beam leaves parallel to the way it came in. A single mirror cannot do this for all angles.

items.p: Put these in order of how much of the light that lands on them they send back, from the least to the most.
items.why: Black cloth sends back a small share. The Moon sends back about one eighth. White paper sends back most of the light. A good mirror sends back about nine tenths.

items.p: Using the words bumps and wavelength, explain why a polished steel plate shows a clear picture but a scratched one shows a hazy picture.
items.a: Light behaves as a wave of about half a thousandth of a millimetre long. A polished plate has bumps much smaller than that, so the light sees a flat surface and reflects in order. A scratched plate has bigger bumps and scratches facing every way, so some of the light scatters, and the picture is hazy.
items.why: A strong answer connects the size of the bumps to the size of the wavelength.

items.p: An optical fibre carries a flash of light round a bend inside a thin strand of glass. How does the light stay inside?
opts: It bounces off the inside walls and does not escape
It is pushed by the glass
It goes through the walls and comes back
It turns into heat and then back into light
items.why: When light hits the glass wall at a shallow angle from the inside, all of it is reflected back in. It zigzags down the strand. This is called total internal reflection.

items.p: Draw two mirrors at a right angle, a ray coming in and the ray going out. Show that the outgoing ray is parallel to the incoming ray.
items.a: Two lines at a right angle, like the corner of a box, with the shiny sides facing in. A ray comes in, hits one mirror, then the other, and leaves going back parallel to the way it came in, with arrows drawn on each.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two bounces and an outgoing ray that is parallel to the incoming ray.
items.art: Two lines meeting at a right angle on a blank page, with no rays drawn.

items.p: A beam meets a flat mirror and makes an angle of 20 degrees with the surface. At what angle to the surface does it leave?
items.why: The beam leaves at the same angle at which it arrived. So it leaves at 20 degrees to the surface.

items.p: A famous story says Archimedes burned the Roman ships at Syracuse with mirrors. Three people discuss it.

views.says: Writers said it happened, so it must be true.
Ships move, the Sun is not a tiny dot, and the spot is hard to hold. It would be very hard to do.
The earliest writers on the siege do not mention it. The story appears much later.

items.ask: What evidence would convince you that the story is true? Choose a view, say why, and say one thing another view gets right.
items.a: A strong answer asks for evidence from the time, such as writing from people who were there, or tests that set a moving ship on fire. It credits the scientist's point about moving ships or the teacher's point about late writers.
items.why: A strong answer separates a story being told from a story being shown, and says what evidence would settle it.

items.p: Three of these send light back in an orderly way. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: A still pond
A polished steel thali
A polished marble floor
A cotton shirt
items.why: The pond, the thali and the marble are smooth, so they reflect in order. The cotton shirt is rough and scatters the light.

items.p: A wet pebble looks shinier than a dry pebble. What is the best reason?
opts: Water fills the tiny dips, so the surface is smoother
Water makes the pebble heavier
Water adds colour to the pebble
Water makes its own light
items.why: The dips in the dry stone scatter the light. The water fills them with a smooth top, so more light reflects in order.

items.p: Reflecting sunlight away from the Earth would remove the extra carbon dioxide in the air. True or false?
items.why: False. Reflecting sunlight might cool the Earth a little, but the carbon dioxide would still be in the air. This is one reason many scientists say we should cut the gases first.

items.p: A sheet of white paper looks equally bright from every side of a room. What is the best reason?
opts: It scatters light in every direction
It makes its own light
It is a mirror
It takes in the light
items.why: The fibres in paper face every way, so light leaves in every direction. Wherever you stand, some reaches your eyes. A mirror would look bright from only one place.

items.p: A convex mirror makes things look bigger than they really are. True or false?
items.why: False. A convex mirror curves outward and shows a wide view, so each thing in it looks smaller. A concave mirror held close can make things look bigger.

items.p: A set of three mirrors at right angles, like the corner of a box, that sends light straight back is called a ____.
items.why: A retroreflector sends light back the way it came. It is used in bicycle reflectors, cat's eyes and road signs, and on the Moon.

items.p: Match each person to what they found out.
pairs: Isaac Newton, 1668
built a reflecting telescope with a curved mirror
Michael Land, 1965
showed that scallops have mirrors in their eyes
Narinder Singh Kapany, 1950s
early work on carrying light along glass fibres
Ibn al-Haytham, about 1021
argued that light comes into the eye from things
items.why: Each person added a piece to the story of how light is reflected, bent and carried.

items.p: Sort these. Does the surface reflect in order, or scatter?
items.why: Orderly reflection needs a very smooth surface. Brick, skin and wool have bumps and fuzz that face every way.

items.p: Explain why a periscope shows the picture the right way round, although it uses two mirrors.
items.a: Each flat mirror flips the picture once. The first mirror flips it and the second flips it back. Two flips cancel each other, so the picture arrives upright and not reversed.
items.why: A strong answer says each mirror flips the picture, and the two flips cancel.

items.p: A cat's eyes glow green in a torch beam at night. What is the best reason?
opts: A mirror layer behind the cat's retina sends light back out through the eye
The cat's eyes make their own light
The cat's eyes are made of glass
The torch beam heats the cat's eyes
items.why: The mirror layer gives light a second chance to be caught by the eye, which helps a cat see in dim light. Some of it comes back out, and you see it as a glow. Picking 'the cat's eyes make their own light' mixes up reflecting with making light.

items.p: Draw a concave mirror and three parallel rays coming in. Show where the rays go after they bounce.
items.a: A curved mirror with the hollow side facing the rays. Three parallel rays arrive. After bouncing, all three cross at one point in front of the mirror, called the focus.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the rays meeting at one point, because each tiny patch of the curve tilts a little differently.
items.art: A curved mirror shape on the right side of an empty page, with three horizontal arrows pointing at it.

items.p: The Earth is warming. Some people suggest sending some sunlight back into space, for example with tiny shiny particles high in the air.

views.who: A scientist who wants it studied
views.says: We should study it now, so that we have the facts if things get worse.
It might change the monsoon in ways we cannot predict, and if it stopped suddenly, the Earth would warm quickly.
The first job is to cut the gases that cause the warming. Reflecting sunlight should come only after that.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, and say one thing another view gets right.
items.a: There is no single right answer. A strong answer gives a clear reason, such as caring about the monsoon, or wanting the facts, and admits that another view raises a good point.
items.why: This question is about how to weigh a risk against a benefit. A strong answer considers who would be affected.

items.p: A beam travelling right meets a mirror leaning right, like a slash. It turns upward and then meets a mirror leaning left, like a backslash. Which way does it go after the second mirror?
opts: Left
Right
Up
Down
items.why: A beam going up that meets a backslash turns to the left. Picture a ball flying up at a backslash. It is knocked off to the left. The first mirror turned the beam from right to up, and the second turns it from up to left.

items.p: Put these in order from the roughest surface to the smoothest.
items.why: Brick has big bumps, paper has small fibres, varnish fills most bumps and a mirror is smooth to a tiny fraction of a wavelength.

items.p: Fog on a mirror is a layer of tiny drops that scatter the light. True or false?
items.why: True. Each drop is a tiny curved bump that sends light off in its own direction. The glass underneath is still smooth, but the picture is gone until the drops clear.

items.p: You have a torch and a sheet of kitchen foil. Describe a test to find out whether crumpling the foil changes where it sends the light. Say what you would keep the same and what you would look for.
items.a: Shine the torch at the smooth foil from a fixed angle and distance, and look from several places to see where the lit spot is bright. Then crumple the foil and repeat with the same torch, angle and distance. Keep the torch and the viewing places the same. Look for whether the light now reaches more places and looks sparkly.
items.why: A strong answer changes only one thing, the crumpling, and says what difference to look for.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a periscope. Label the four parts: the top window, the top mirror, the lower mirror and the lower window.
a: top window: where the light from the scene comes in
top mirror: turns the light down the tube
lower mirror: turns the light toward the viewer
lower window: where the viewer looks
items.why: The windows are on opposite faces of the tube. The mirrors lean the same way, and their shiny sides face each other.
items.art: A tall periscope tube with two empty window openings, two mirrors inside, and four empty label boxes.

items.p: Why is it dangerous to use a curved shaving mirror to shine sunlight onto your hand?
opts: The mirror gathers the sunlight into a spot hot enough to burn
The mirror makes new sunlight
The mirror spreads the light too thin
The mirror is too heavy
items.why: A concave mirror gathers light to a focus. The light there is packed tight and turns into heat when it lands on skin. It can burn, start a fire or harm eyes. Always use a torch for experiments, never sunlight.

items.p: A reflective strip on a school bag looks very bright in daylight and dim in a car's headlights. True or false?
items.why: False. A reflective strip sends light straight back to its source. It glows brightly when a headlight or torch shines on it, as seen from near the light. In ordinary daylight it looks plain, because the light comes from everywhere and not back toward your eyes.

quiz.p: A narrow beam of light lands on a mirror and on a sheet of white paper at the same angle. What is different about the light that leaves?
opts: From the mirror it leaves in one direction, and from the paper it leaves in many directions
From the mirror it leaves in many directions, and from the paper in one direction
Both send it off in exactly the same direction
Neither sends any light back
quiz.why: A mirror is smooth, so all the rays leave together in one direction. Paper is rough, so the rays go off in many directions. Both reflect, which is why you can see the lit spot on the paper from anywhere.

quiz.p: The rule of reflection works on every tiny patch of a surface. So why does a rough surface still scatter the light?
opts: The tiny patches are tilted every way, so each ray leaves in its own direction
The rule stops working on rough surfaces
Rough surfaces take in all the light
Rough surfaces turn light into sound
quiz.why: Each tiny patch follows the rule, but the patches face different ways. So the rays leave at different angles. Nothing is broken. Picking 'the rule stops working' is a common idea, but the rule holds on every patch.

quiz.p: Which treatment would make a dull piece of card show the clearest reflection of a lamp?
opts: Covering it with smooth clear tape
Scratching it with sandpaper
Crumpling it
Painting it with matt paint
quiz.why: Clear tape lays a very flat skin over the bumps, so the surface is smooth. The other three make the bumps bigger or leave them as they are.

quiz.p: A calm lake shows the trees almost perfectly at sunrise, but shows them poorly at noon. What helps most at sunrise?
opts: The Sun is low, so we see the water at a low angle, and calm water is smooth
The lake is deeper at sunrise
The lake is warmer at sunrise
The trees are taller at sunrise
quiz.why: A low angle makes any surface reflect more in order, and calm water is smooth already. Together they make a clear picture. Seen from high above at noon, the same lake reflects less of the sky.

quiz.p: How many mirrors does a simple periscope have, and how are they set?
opts: Two, each tilted at 45 degrees, with their shiny sides facing each other
One, tilted at 90 degrees
Three, each pointing at the viewer
Two, one flat on the floor and one on the ceiling
quiz.why: A mirror tilted at 45 degrees turns a ray through a right angle. Two of them, one at each end of a tube, turn the ray twice, so you can look over a wall.

quiz.p: A periscope with just one mirror, instead of two, would show a picture that is
opts: Reversed, because one flip is not cancelled
Upright, the same as with two mirrors
Upside down
Twice as bright
quiz.why: Each flat mirror flips the picture front to back once. With two mirrors, the two flips cancel. With one mirror, the flip stays and the picture is reversed.

quiz.p: A cat's eye in the road and a bicycle reflector both glow in a car's headlights. What do they have in common?
opts: Both have tiny corner mirrors that send light straight back toward the light
Both make their own light
Both are made of the same metal
Both only work in daylight
quiz.why: Corner mirrors at right angles send light back the way it came. The driver's eyes are near the headlights, so the driver sees the glow.

quiz.p: A shopkeeper wants one mirror that shows the whole shop. Which kind is best?
opts: A convex mirror, which curves outward
A concave mirror, which curves inward
A flat mirror
No mirror shows more than a flat mirror
quiz.why: A convex mirror collects light from a wide range of directions, so it shows a wide view, in a smaller size. A concave mirror held far from the face would turn the picture upside down, and shows a narrower view.

quiz.p: A solar cooker has a curved shiny dish. What does the dish do?
opts: It gathers sunlight onto the pot
It makes new sunlight
It spreads sunlight over the whole kitchen
It turns sunlight into sound
quiz.why: A concave dish tilts each patch so that the reflected rays cross at the pot. The light is packed into a small area, which heats the pot. Dangerous for eyes and skin, so never aim one at a person.

quiz.p: Isaac Newton built a telescope with a curved mirror instead of a big lens. What problem did this avoid?
opts: Coloured fringes, because a mirror bounces every colour at the same angle
The telescope being too heavy
The stars being too bright
The Moon being too far away
quiz.why: Glass bends colours by different amounts, so lenses give coloured fringes. A mirror reflects all colours alike. Newton showed this about 1666 with a prism.

quiz.p: A torch lights only a red card. A white card next to it looks slightly pink near the fold. What does this show?
opts: Light can bounce twice, and it carries colour from the first surface to the second
White paper turns pink in the dark
The torch is red
Red cards make their own light
quiz.why: The red card scatters red light onto the white card, which scatters it again into your eyes. Every surface reflects, so light can bounce from one surface to another.

quiz.p: A friend says, 'A wall does not reflect light, because it shows no picture of me.' What is the best reply?
opts: You can see the wall only because it reflects light into your eyes. It scatters the light, so there is no picture
You are right, a wall takes in all the light
A wall makes its own light
Walls only reflect in the dark
quiz.why: A wall reflects light in every direction, so it is visible from anywhere. What it lacks is the tidy order that makes a picture.

Solar cookers use shiny dishes to gather sunlight onto a pot.

Optical fibres carry internet messages as flashes of light under the sea.
Polish, wax and varnish make shoes, cars and furniture shine.
A signal mirror can flash sunlight across a long distance to call for help.

open_questions.q: Could we build a mirror so smooth and so large that it makes a telescope as sharp as we dream of?
open_questions.why_open: Telescope mirrors are getting bigger, but big mirrors bend under their own weight and the air above them blurs the view. Engineers are still finding ways round these limits.

open_questions.q: Should the world try to reflect sunlight away to cool the Earth?
open_questions.why_open: The ideas have not been tested at scale, and no one knows what they would do to the monsoon or to the world's weather. Scientists and countries disagree.

open_questions.q: Why do only some animals recognise their own face in a mirror?
open_questions.why_open: A few kinds of animals pass the mark test. Scientists disagree about whether failing it means an animal has no sense of self, or only that the test does not suit them.

open_questions.q: Can we make a surface that reflects no light at all?
open_questions.why_open: The blackest materials take in more than 99.9 parts in 100 of the light, but none is perfect. Scientists do not agree on whether a perfect one can exist.

open_questions.q: Could a cloak bend light round a person to make them invisible?
open_questions.why_open: Special materials can bend some kinds of light round small objects in a laboratory. Nobody has made a cloak for a person that works for all the colours.

open_questions.q: What is the best shape for a mirror that gathers sunlight over a whole day without moving?
open_questions.why_open: The Sun moves across the sky, so most solar mirrors need to be turned. Engineers keep searching for cheaper shapes that follow the Sun without moving parts.

maths.problem: A mirror reflects 9 out of every 10 parts of the light that lands on it. White paper reflects 8 out of every 10 parts. Black cloth reflects 1 out of every 20 parts. If 400 units of light land on each, how many units does each one reflect?
maths.answer: The mirror reflects 360 units, the paper 320 units and the black cloth 20 units.
maths.explain: For the mirror, a tenth of 400 is 40, and 9 times 40 is 360. For the paper, 8 times 40 is 320. For the cloth, a twentieth of 400 is 20. So the mirror reflects the most and the cloth the least.
maths.context: You tested six surfaces in Where Does the Bounce Go. These are made-up numbers for how much light each surface might send back.
maths.why_maths: Taking a fraction of the light lands on a surface tells you how much it sends back, so you can compare surfaces with numbers.

maths.problem: A beam of light lands on a flat mirror and makes an angle of 30 degrees with the surface. It leaves at the same angle on the other side. What is the angle between the beam going in and the beam going out?
maths.explain: Along the surface of the mirror there is a straight line of 180 degrees. The beam going in uses 30 degrees at one end, and the beam going out uses 30 degrees at the other. 180 take away 30 take away 30 is 120.
maths.context: In Where Does the Bounce Go, you aimed a thin beam at a mirror and looked for the place where the flash came out. Here is a sum about those angles.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the two equal angles from a straight line tells you where to look for the bounce before you test.

maths.problem: A mirror at 45 degrees turns a beam through 90 degrees. A beam passes through four such mirrors in a row, and each one turns it 90 degrees in the same direction. How many degrees does the beam turn in total, and which way is it going at the end?
maths.answer: 360 degrees in total. It is going the same way it started.
maths.explain: 4 times 90 is 360. A full turn is 360 degrees. So after four turns in the same direction, the beam is back to its starting direction.
maths.context: In Mirror Maze, a beam turns a right angle at each mirror. Here the beam meets four mirrors, all turning the same way.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the turns shows that four right angles make a full circle, which helps you predict where a beam will end up.

maths.problem: A butterfly shape has one line of symmetry down the middle. If you stand a mirror along that line, the left wing and its reflection make the whole butterfly. The left wing is 6 centimetres wide at its widest. How wide is the whole butterfly?
maths.explain: A mirror along the line of symmetry shows a reflection of the left wing that is the same width. 6 plus 6 is 12. So the whole butterfly is 12 centimetres wide.
maths.context: A mirror makes a picture that is the same size as the thing and on the opposite side. Here is a shape with a line of symmetry.
maths.why_maths: A line of symmetry is where a mirror would work, so doubling half a shape gives the whole shape.

maths.problem: Each of the two card wedges for the Milk-Carton Periscope is a strip 7 centimetres wide and 24 centimetres long. How much card do you need for one wedge, and for both?
maths.answer: 168 square centimetres for one wedge, and 336 square centimetres for both.
maths.explain: 7 times 24 is 7 times 20, which is 140, plus 7 times 4, which is 28. 140 plus 28 is 168. Two wedges need 168 times 2, which is 336.
maths.context: In the Milk-Carton Periscope project, you fold two card strips into wedges. Here is how much card you need.
maths.why_maths: Working out the area before you cut shows whether one sheet of card is enough for both wedges.

maths.problem: The Moon sends back about 12 parts in every 100 of the sunlight that lands on it. White paper sends back about 80 parts in every 100. About how many times as much light does white paper send back as the Moon, for the same light landing?
maths.explain: 80 divided by 12 is a little more than 6 and a half. 12 times 6 is 72, and 12 times 7 is 84. So 80 is a bit less than 7 times 12. We say about 7 times.
maths.context: You learned that the Moon is dark grey and sends back only a small share of sunlight. Here is how the Moon compares with white paper.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one share by the other tells you how many times brighter one surface is than another, using the same light.

maths.problem: In Where Does the Bounce Go, six surfaces were tested. The mirror was seen from 1 of the 5 marks, the smooth foil 1, the crumpled foil 5, the white paper 5, the black cloth 2 and the glossy page 5. What fraction of the surfaces could be seen from all 5 marks?
maths.answer: One half, which is 3 of the 6 surfaces.
maths.explain: The crumpled foil, the white paper and the glossy page were seen from all 5 marks. That is 3 surfaces out of 6. 3 out of 6 is the same as one half. These are made-up results.
maths.context: In Where Does the Bounce Go, you counted the marks from which each surface showed a lit spot. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Writing a fraction from the table shows at a glance how many of the surfaces scatter light in every direction.

maths.problem: A laser flash goes to the reflectors on the Moon and back in about 2 and a half seconds. So the flash takes 1 and a quarter seconds each way. Light goes about 3 lakh kilometres in one second. About how far away is the Moon?
maths.explain: 1 and a quarter seconds is 1 second plus a quarter second. In 1 second light goes 3,00,000 kilometres. A quarter of 3,00,000 is 75,000. 3,00,000 plus 75,000 is 3,75,000 kilometres. The real distance changes a little as the Moon moves.
maths.context: You learned that astronauts left corner reflectors on the Moon, which send laser flashes straight back. Here is how to use the time to find the distance.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the time by the speed of light turns a time you can measure into a distance you could never walk.

The mirror's flash is at mark 4, and a phone torch can dazzle, so the steps say to glance only. The five marks and the 45 degree torch mark were worked out from the rule of reflection.
